#5726. Scientists discover why chronic back pain feels so personal

For people living with chronic back pain, even a simple movement can trigger a sudden surge of pain. Now, scientists have discovered that these painful episodes activate a surprising part of the brain, one closely connected to our sense of identity and how we think about ourselves.

Researchers at UC San Diego School of Medicine found that movement-triggered pain in people with chronic low back pain (cLBP) activates a brain network that normally becomes less active during ordinary pain. The discovery suggests that persistent back pain may become deeply intertwined with a person's sense of self, potentially helping explain why conventional pain treatments often provide limited relief.

According to the World Health Organization, low back pain is the leading cause of disability worldwide. When pain persists for more than 12 weeks, it is considered chronic. For many patients, everyday movements can provoke sudden flare-ups that make an already difficult condition even harder to manage.

Although the brain plays a central role in how pain is experienced, researchers have struggled to identify the precise brain circuits responsible for pain triggered by movement.

Chronic Back Pain Activates the Brain's Sense of Self

The new study, published on October 5, 2026, in the British Journal of Anaesthesia, identified an unexpected response involving the brain's Default Mode Network (DMN).

Sometimes called the "self network," the DMN consists of interconnected regions in the frontal, parietal, and temporal lobes. These areas are especially active when our attention turns inward, such as when we reflect on personal experiences, think about our identity, or consider our thoughts and emotions. In contrast, the network generally becomes less active when we direct our attention toward something happening around us.

The researchers discovered that sudden back pain caused by movement switched this network on rather than off. This unusual response suggests that chronic pain involves more than the processing of physical sensations. It may also engage the brain systems that shape how people experience themselves.

The findings could help researchers understand why treatments that focus primarily on suppressing pain symptoms do not always work well for chronic low back pain. They also raise the possibility that targeting the DMN could offer a different approach to treatment.

Brain Scans Reveal a Surprising Difference Between Chronic and Acute Pain

To investigate what happens in the brain during a pain flare, the researchers recruited 114 patients with chronic low back pain.

Each participant completed a "leg raise test," a standard clinical procedure used to provoke back pain. During the test, researchers monitored changes in brain blood flow using a specialized functional MRI method called arterial spin labeling. This technique allows scientists to track patterns of brain activity by measuring blood flow without relying on an injected contrast agent.

The team also examined how participants responded to a separate painful stimulus. They applied a harmless but uncomfortable heat sensation to the calf, similar to the brief pain someone might experience when accidentally touching a hot stove.

Comparing these two situations revealed a striking difference.

When movement triggered a flare of chronic back pain, the DMN became more active. However, when participants experienced the painful heat stimulus, the same network became less active, following the brain's typical response to acute pain.

The researchers also identified several other important patterns:

Together, these findings provide new evidence that chronic pain flares involve brain processes associated with personal identity, not just the physical experience of pain.

Why the Brain Reacts Differently to Chronic Pain

During ordinary acute pain, the brain generally reduces activity in the DMN so it can concentrate on the immediate source of danger. This response helps shift attention away from internal thoughts and toward an external threat.

But the UC San Diego researchers found that movement triggered chronic back pain produced the opposite effect.

"In every pain study, when you're experiencing pain, the DMN deactivates," said corresponding author Fadel Zeidan, PhD, professor in the Department of Anesthesiology, endowed professor at the Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion, and director of the Pain Health and Mindfulness Laboratory at UC San Diego School of Medicine. "What we show for the first time ever is that when you have a pain flare, it turns on instead. You start to identify the experience with who you are."

The findings suggest that chronic back pain can become closely connected with the brain's internal representation of the self. Rather than processing pain solely as a physical warning signal, the brain may also link it to personal memories, expectations, and emotional experiences.

For someone living with chronic pain, this means the experience can extend far beyond the moments when the pain is physically present. Worry about the next flare, memories of previous episodes, and fear of movements that might trigger pain can all become part of everyday life.

"The moment-to-moment experience is contaminated not only by the feeling of pain, but by the anticipation of it and recovery from it. It's contaminated by past experiences like embarrassment about not being able to participate in normal activities and fear of movement when trying to avoid the pain."

This connection between pain and personal identity may help explain why chronic back pain can be especially difficult to treat.

A New Direction for Chronic Back Pain Treatment

Because movement-triggered chronic back pain engages different brain networks from ordinary acute pain, researchers believe traditional treatments may fail to address some of the processes that sustain the experience of chronic pain.

Medications such as opiates primarily target pain signaling, but they may not adequately address the brain networks involved in the emotional and personal dimensions of persistent pain.

"Current pain medicine is fixated on ridding patients of their pain symptoms, but that's not the source of chronic pain. These data suggest that a chronic pain flare also encompasses one's identity."

The discovery points toward treatments that address not only the sensation of pain but also the brain's relationship with that sensation.

Recent work by Zeidan and his colleagues has explored two potential approaches: mindfulness meditation and the psychedelic compound psilocybin.

Both approaches are being investigated for their ability to help people experience physical pain without allowing it to become as closely tied to their identity. Early findings suggest that changing this relationship may reduce pain intensity, although additional research is needed to confirm the results and determine how effective these treatments may be.

"These types of mind-body and psychedelic medicine approaches target the whole person," Zeidan said. "Mindfulness is a meditation technique that's about cultivating non-judgmental awareness of the present moment that dramatically reduces pain in a very unique way. Psilocybin seemingly resets the pain system that integrates trauma, past experiences and future worries to facilitate a restart, if you will. They're not a silver bullet -- you're not necessarily getting rid of the pain, but you're changing the relationship you have with that pain so it doesn't contaminate your everyday life."

Can Mindfulness and Psychedelics Change How the Brain Experiences Pain?

Rather than attempting to eliminate every pain signal, these approaches aim to change how the brain interprets and responds to the experience.

Mindfulness meditation encourages people to observe their thoughts, emotions, and physical sensations without immediately judging or reacting to them. Psilocybin, meanwhile, is being studied for its potential to alter brain processes that connect pain with earlier experiences, emotional distress, and expectations about the future.

The goal is not necessarily to remove pain altogether, but to reduce how much it influences a person's thoughts, emotions, and daily functioning.

Zeidan's laboratory is currently conducting several clinical trials using brain imaging to investigate whether mindfulness meditation and psychedelic treatments can change the neural processes involved in self-reflection. Researchers hope to determine whether these approaches can reshape brain activity and improve how people subjectively experience chronic pain.

Although the research remains at an early stage, the findings offer a different way to think about persistent back pain. Understanding why the brain connects chronic pain with a person's sense of self could eventually help scientists develop treatments that address aspects of pain that conventional therapies often miss.

Additional study authors from UC San Diego School of Medicine include Morgan Gianola, Jon Dean, Conan Chen, Daniel Barrows, Gabriel Reigner, and Thomas Liu.

Funding was provided in part by the National Institutes of Health's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health (Grant #R01AT009693) and the UC San Diego Sanford Institute for Empathy and Compassion. The researchers reported no conflicts of interest.

#5723. Less than 42 minutes of bright daylight linked to higher dementia risk

Could the amount of daylight you get each day offer clues about your risk of developing dementia? A large new study suggests that exposure to brighter daytime light is associated with a lower likelihood of developing the condition.

The findings, published in General Psychiatry, point to daytime light exposure as a potentially overlooked factor in brain health.

Brighter Daylight Linked to Lower Dementia Risk

To investigate the connection, researchers analyzed data from 87,577 adults who wore wrist devices equipped with accelerometers. The devices allowed scientists to measure participants' exposure to light during both the day and night. Over a median follow-up period of 8.1 years, 741 participants developed dementia.

The results revealed a notable pattern. People exposed to average daytime light levels exceeding 1,000 lux (a moderately bright light level equivalent to an overcast day outdoors) had a 16% lower risk of developing dementia. Spending longer periods in even brighter daytime light (at least 5,000 lux) was associated with further reductions in risk.

Too Little Daylight Emerges as a Surprising Dementia Risk Indicator

One of the most striking findings involved people who received very little bright light during the day. Getting less than 0.7 hours, or 42 minutes, of bright daytime light daily was a stronger predictor of dementia than 6 established dementia risk factors.

Interestingly, researchers found no statistically significant connection between nighttime light exposure and dementia risk. This suggests that daytime brightness, rather than light exposure at night, may be particularly relevant to the relationship identified in the study.

"Daytime light exposure may serve as a novel indicator of dementia risk," said corresponding author Hongliang Feng, PhD, of Guangzhou Medical University, in China.

Although the findings reveal an association, they do not establish that getting more daylight directly prevents dementia. Instead, the research highlights daytime light exposure as a potentially valuable indicator of dementia risk that deserves further investigation.

#5720. Why some “lower-risk” childhood cancers turn deadly

Some childhood cancers may be far more dangerous than their initial risk classification suggests. Scientists have discovered that certain tumors considered less threatening can contain hidden populations of highly aggressive cancer cells, potentially explaining why some children experience devastating outcomes despite lacking the usual genetic warning signs.

The discovery could change how doctors identify children at risk of life-threatening cancer, allowing treatment to be better matched to the true aggressiveness of their disease.

The findings, published in Cancer Research, come from scientists at the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the University of Cambridge, Great Ormond Street Hospital (GOSH), University College London, and collaborating institutions. Their research focused on rhabdomyosarcoma (RMS), an aggressive cancer that develops from muscle tissue and is among the most common soft tissue cancers affecting children younger than 15. Approximately 55 children are diagnosed with the disease in the United Kingdom each year.[1]

Unlike many adult cancers, which can develop after years of aging or exposure to environmental factors, childhood cancers often result from genetic changes that occur during early development.

Why Some Childhood Cancers Defy Risk Predictions

Doctors generally divide rhabdomyosarcoma into two main categories based on whether a tumor carries a particular genetic warning sign. This marker occurs when two genes that are normally separate become fused together, creating an abnormal genetic combination associated with especially aggressive disease.[2]

Children whose tumors contain this fusion have substantially lower survival rates than those without it, even when they receive intensive treatment.

But this classification has a troubling limitation. Some children whose tumors lack the high-risk genetic marker still develop aggressive cancers that can prove fatal. Until now, scientists have struggled to explain why these supposedly less dangerous tumors sometimes behave so aggressively.

To investigate this mystery, the research team compared tumors from children with different forms of rhabdomyosarcoma, looking beyond the genetic markers traditionally used to estimate risk.

The researchers examined tumor samples from 16 children, including four whose cancers lacked the fusion marker but proved fatal, four with fusion-positive tumors, and eight children with fusion-negative disease who remained alive.

Using advanced genetic analysis, scientists studied the tumors at a level of detail that conventional techniques cannot easily achieve.

One of their main tools was single-cell RNA sequencing, a technology that measures gene activity in individual cells. Rather than examining a tumor as a single mass, this approach allows researchers to investigate the behavior of its different cell populations and identify potentially dangerous cells that might otherwise go unnoticed.

The scientists also used spatial transcriptomics, a technique that maps gene activity to specific locations within a tumor. This provided a clearer picture of where aggressive cancer cells were concentrated and how they were distributed throughout the tissue.

The results revealed a striking similarity between tumors that had previously been placed in different risk categories. Some cancers classified as non-high-risk contained cells with gene activity patterns closely resembling those found in high-risk tumors.

Even more surprisingly, these aggressive tumors did not need the same genetic mutations to produce similar behavior. Researchers identified rare genetic changes that affected many of the same cellular pathways involved in the most dangerous forms of the disease.

This suggests that different genetic abnormalities can ultimately push cancer cells toward a shared aggressive state. In other words, tumors can reach a similarly dangerous biological condition through multiple genetic routes, even when they lack the warning sign typically used to identify high-risk disease.

Dr. Karin Straathof, co-senior author at UCL Cancer Institute and GOSH, said:

"By studying tumors one cell at a time, we uncovered hidden populations of aggressive cancer cells that conventional methods miss. Although these tumors carry different genetic changes, many converge on the same aggressive pathways. This helps explain why some children who appear to have lower-risk disease can still have a devastating outcome."

A New Path Toward More Precise Cancer Treatment

The findings could have important implications for how childhood cancer is diagnosed and treated.

If doctors can identify the distinctive biological signatures of aggressive cancer cells at diagnosis, they may be able to recognize children who face a greater risk of relapse or death, even when standard genetic tests suggest otherwise.

Such an approach could also help prevent unnecessary treatment. Children with genuinely lower-risk tumors might avoid some of the harmful side effects associated with intensive chemotherapy, while those with hidden aggressive disease could receive stronger or more targeted treatment earlier.

The researchers are particularly interested in identifying markers that could be used to develop therapies aimed specifically at the most dangerous cancer cells.

One possible direction involves immunotherapy, including CAR-T cell therapy. This treatment uses specially modified immune cells to recognize and attack cancer cells. Although such treatments would require further development and testing for rhabdomyosarcoma, they could eventually offer a more precise alternative to conventional chemotherapy, potentially reducing damage to healthy tissues.

Scientists are now expanding their research to include hundreds of additional tumor samples. By studying a much larger group of patients, they hope to uncover more of the rare genetic changes capable of producing aggressive cancer and accelerate the development of personalized treatments.

Sara Wakeling, Chief Executive Officer and co-founder of Alice's Arc, said:

"Every child with cancer deserves the best possible chance of survival. We're proud to support research into rhabdomyosarcoma, showing how cutting-edge technologies can uncover the biology driving aggressive childhood cancers. These discoveries bring us closer to more personalized treatments and better outcomes for children."

Dr. Laura Danielson, Children's and Young Person's Lead at Cancer Research UK, said:

"Discovery research like this is essential to understand the unique biology of these cancers. This important study demonstrates that aggressive tumors may share similar features, even if they carry different genetic changes. By helping researchers understand what these high-risk cancers have in common, this work adds a vital piece to the puzzle and could help guide future efforts to improve treatment for children and young people with rhabdomyosarcoma."

Rethinking How Doctors Identify Dangerous Childhood Cancers

Beyond its potential treatment applications, the discovery challenges a fundamental assumption about how rhabdomyosarcoma should be classified.

Instead of viewing aggressive disease primarily through the presence or absence of one genetic abnormality, the researchers suggest that doctors may need to consider the broader biological state of the cancer cells themselves.

This distinction is important because tumors with different mutations can behave in remarkably similar ways. Identifying the shared features of aggressive disease could provide a more reliable way to recognize children who need intensive treatment, regardless of the particular genetic changes driving their tumors.

Professor Sam Behjati, co-senior author formerly at the Wellcome Sanger Institute and Head of the Department of Paediatrics at the University of Cambridge, said:

"This work changes how we think about rhabdomyosarcoma. Rather than a single, abnormal gene, we've shown that there is an overarching cell state of aggressive disease that defies conventional classification systems. Understanding this shared biology could help identify children who need more intense treatment to improve their survival."

Although further research is needed before these findings can change routine clinical care, they provide a promising foundation for more accurate risk assessments and treatments tailored to each child's cancer.

By revealing aggressive behavior hidden beneath seemingly reassuring genetic classifications, scientists hope to improve survival for children with the most dangerous tumors while sparing others from treatment they may not need.

The research received support through a Cancer Research UK -- Children with Cancer UK Innovation Award, with additional co-funding from Alice's Arc and funding from Wellcome.

#5719. Type 2 diabetes breakthrough as 54% achieve remission in just 6 months

A carefully structured combination of diet and exercise may offer a powerful way to put type 2 diabetes into remission in younger adults. In a new clinical trial, more than half of participants who followed an intensive lifestyle program achieved remission within just six months, compared with only 4% of those receiving standard care.

The findings, presented at the Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas, suggest that a low-calorie diet paired with regular exercise could significantly change the course of early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) (aged under 45 years).

The research was conducted by Professor Kaberi Dasgupta, Director of the Division of General Internal Medicine at McGill University in Montreal, Canada, Professor Thomas Yates of the University of Leicester in the UK, and their colleagues.

Why Early-Onset Type 2 Diabetes Is Especially Dangerous

Type 2 diabetes diagnosed at a younger age can be particularly aggressive. People with early-onset type 2 diabetes (EOT2D) often experience a faster decline in blood sugar control, develop complications earlier in life, and face a shorter life expectancy than those diagnosed at older ages.

Previous research has shown that very low-calorie diets (LEDs) can lower blood sugar enough for some people to achieve remission without diabetes medication (T2D remission). Remission means blood sugar has fallen below the threshold used to diagnose diabetes and remains there without glucose-lowering drugs. However, it does not necessarily mean the disease has been permanently cured.

Researchers wanted to find out whether adding structured exercise could make this approach even more effective. Beyond helping regulate blood sugar, physical activity could improve fitness, protect muscle during weight loss, strengthen heart function, and reduce insulin resistance.

To investigate, the team tested whether combining a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise could achieve remission after 24 weeks, compared with standard medical care.

The randomized clinical trial took place at three research centers in England and Canada (affiliated with the University of Leicester, UK, McGill University (Montreal), and the University of Alberta, Edmonton). It enrolled adults aged 18 to 45 who had early-onset type 2 diabetes and obesity but were not using insulin.

The trial was open-label, meaning participants and researchers knew which treatment each person received, although the assessment of the main outcome was blinded.

One group continued receiving usual care. The other followed an intensive program that combined a daily intake of 800 to 900 calories with supervised aerobic and resistance exercise twice per week, plus one independent exercise session each week (weeks 1-12). Participants then transitioned to a diet designed to maintain their weight loss while continuing to exercise independently (weeks 13-24).

The researchers measured how many participants achieved diabetes remission after 24 weeks. To qualify, participants needed an HbA1c level below 6.5%, equivalent to 48 mmol/mol, and must have taken no glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks. HbA1c is a blood test that reflects average blood sugar levels over approximately three months.

The analysis included everyone assigned to either group. When remission data were missing, researchers conservatively counted those participants as not having achieved remission. They also examined changes in cardiovascular fitness, body composition, and heart structure.

At the beginning of the intensive program, participants discontinued medications used to lower blood sugar and blood pressure (in the absence of albuminuria), under the study's medical supervision. Albuminuria refers to the presence of a protein called albumin in urine and can indicate kidney damage.

Their restricted diet provided 800 to 900 calories daily (30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, 20% fat). Participants were encouraged to drink at least two liters of calorie-free fluids each day and were given access to a fiber-based laxative when needed.

During the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). From weeks three through 12, participants maintained the same calorie limit but gained more flexibility in their food choices (Optifast in UK and ProtiDiet in Canada).

This second phase allowed one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables (60 to 90 g protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, two portions of non-starchy vegetables).

After the first 12 weeks, participants shifted toward maintaining their weight loss rather than continuing rapid weight reduction.

More Than Half Achieved Type 2 Diabetes Remission

Between September 24, 2021, and June 6, 2025, the researchers enrolled and randomly assigned 96 participants (40 UK, 56 Canada). The group included 50 people assigned to the intensive intervention and 46 receiving standard care (24 female, 26 male intervention group; 21 female, 25 male control group; mean age 38 years, BMI 35·2 kg/m2).

Of those enrolled, 86 (90%) completed the final assessments.

The results revealed a striking difference between the groups. After 24 weeks, 27 of the 50 participants following the diet and exercise program had achieved remission, representing 54% of the intervention group. In comparison, just two of the 46 participants receiving standard care reached remission, or approximately 4%.

After accounting for relevant statistical factors, the researchers calculated that participants in the intensive lifestyle program were 21 times more likely to achieve remission than those receiving usual care.

Weight loss was also substantially greater among participants following the combined program.

Among the 47 intervention participants with available weight data, average body weight fell from 100.7 kg to 92.3 kg, a reduction of 8.4 kg over 24 weeks. The 43 control participants with available weight data started at an average of 103.2 kg and lost just 1.2 kg, reaching 102.0 kg.

After statistical adjustment, the intervention group lost an average of 7.5 kg more weight than the control group. Importantly, this included an additional 6.6 kg of fat loss, indicating that much of the difference came from reduced body fat.

Promising Results With Manageable Side Effects

No severe adverse events were reported during the trial. However, side effects were more common among participants following the intensive diet.

At least one adverse event occurred in 43 of the 50 intervention participants, compared with six of the 46 participants receiving standard care. Most problems appeared during the early stages of the restrictive diet and included symptoms such as constipation, headaches, dizziness, and fatigue (e.g., constipation, headache, dizziness, fatigue). These effects generally resolved.

The researchers believe the findings demonstrate that a combined diet and exercise intervention can produce meaningful improvements beyond blood sugar control alone.

The authors say: "Our findings demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low energy diet in early-onset type 2 diabetes, supporting its potential to deliver substantial and holistic health and well-being benefits alongside diabetes remission.

"Our remission rates are at the upper end of those previously reported in the literature for trials of similar duration, reinforcing the potential of structured lifestyle interventions to support clinically meaningful remission, while demonstrating for the first time that such effects can be achieved in a multi-ethnic population with early-onset type 2 diabetes through a combined low-energy diet and structured exercise intervention."

Why Preserving Muscle During Weight Loss Matters

One particularly important aspect of the study was its emphasis on protecting muscle mass during rapid weight loss.

The researchers explain that most people who complete weight loss programs eventually regain some or all of the weight they lost. This is especially relevant when using very low-calorie diets to achieve diabetes remission.

Losing weight through calorie restriction alone typically reduces both fat and fat-free mass, which includes muscle. Some evidence suggests that when weight returns, the body may regain proportionally more fat than lean tissue.

Over time, repeated weight loss and regain could therefore contribute to a gradual reduction in muscle mass and increase the risk of sarcopenia, a condition characterized by declining muscle mass and strength.

To address this problem, the researchers incorporated resistance training into the most intensive phase of weight loss. Their results suggest that it is possible to achieve substantial fat loss while preserving muscle, potentially making the approach more beneficial for long-term metabolic health.

They say: "Our RESET for Remission study targeted muscle during the intensive weight loss phase through resistance training, and our findings indicate fat-free mass and muscle preservation is achievable with rapid weight loss. Preserving muscle during remission-oriented weight loss may have important implications for long-term metabolic health, physical function, and disease trajectory. This requires examination in a longer-term study."

A Potential New Approach to Treating Type 2 Diabetes

The findings could be particularly important as type 2 diabetes becomes increasingly common among younger adults worldwide.

People who develop the condition earlier in life face more years of exposure to elevated blood sugar, increasing their lifetime risk of cardiovascular disease and other complications. Finding effective ways to achieve remission early could therefore have substantial health benefits.

The researchers emphasize that their intervention did more than lower blood sugar. It also reduced body fat while protecting muscle, improved muscle quality and physical performance, supported cardiovascular health, and produced improvements in participants' reported well-being.

They also suggest that this strategy could be especially relevant for people planning a pregnancy or who may become pregnant.

However, the researchers caution that longer studies are needed to determine whether the benefits can be sustained. In particular, future research must establish how well participants maintain their weight loss, muscle mass, and diabetes remission after returning to everyday life outside a closely monitored clinical trial.

The authors conclude: "By focusing specifically on early-onset type 2 diabetes, our trial addresses a growing clinical population, characterized by elevated cardiovascular disease risk, greater cumulative complication burden, and poor long-term outcomes…In summary, RESET for Remission demonstrated that in early-onset type 2 diabetes, combining structured aerobic and resistance exercise with a low-calorie diet produces high remission rates, induces fat loss while preserving muscle mass, improves muscle quality and function, enhances cardiovascular health, and leads to meaningful improvements in patient-reported outcomes. As the prevalence of early-onset type 2 diabetes rises globally, our findings highlight an opportunity to re-evaluate treatment paradigms and support scalable implementation of integrated dietary and exercise interventions for remission. Our approach may be particularly valuable in those seeking or with potential for pregnancy. It warrants further evaluation in longer term studies in real-world settings."

#5718. Econ Review: A Look at October’s Key Market Data

Editor’s note: Econ Review is a roundup of the housing and economic market data reports released during the month.

As the winter slowdown draws closer, the housing market remains in a sticky spot as the economy continues to face challenges trickling down from the Iran War. Now moving toward the end of 2026, the question remains whether we’ll begin to see a housing market recovery next year.

Let’s take a look at what the housing and economic data reports released in October can show us:

Existing-home sales saw a slight boost as the summer season finally came to a close, up 1.5% month-over-month in the latest report. Some regions picked up as well, with the South and West recording month-over-month gains.

Despite a slight monthly uptick, National Association of Realtors® Chief Economist Lawrence Yun noted in the report that the end of summer—August and September—marked “the two slowest months for home sales this year.”

As such, existing-home sales remained depleted year-over-year by 2.2%. All four regions also saw losses year-over-year.

Ali Wolf, chief economist at NewHomeSource and Zonda, said that the uptick was not an indicator of marker recovery as “supply is still pulling most of the weight here.”

“Today’s report shows a market clearing accumulated listings, not a wave of buyers coming in,” she continued. “And, this is the last clean read before mortgage rates shot up to over 7%, meaning next month we’ll start to see the impact on buyer activity.”

A positive note in the report was a slightly increased share of first-time buyers, as Realtor.com® Chief Economist Danielle Hale said that the market is “past the worst of the starter-home supply crunch nationwide, which may help entry-level buyers gain a foothold.”

In addition, existing-home inventory remains on the rise, growing 1.9% month-over-month and 4.6% year-over-year.

Construction challenges kept new-home sales muted for another month, falling 0.6% month-over-month and 5.3% year-over-year. Additionally, last month’s sales numbers were also revised downward by about 0.6%, dimming activity further.

“Builders continue to offer incentives and adjust pricing to attract buyers, but elevated mortgage rates and high home prices are limiting the number of households that can afford to purchase a home,” said National Association of Home Builders (NAHB) Chairman Bill Owens.

Wolf also predicted a potential increase in new-home sales in the fall and winter due to the incentives being offered by builders to “meet their year-end goals,” making it the “prime season for new home shopping.”

Looking ahead at potential activity, mortgage rates back up in the 7% range are starting to weigh on the market as pending home sales dropped 7.3% month-over-month and 11.3% year-over-year. All four regions also experienced declines on both a monthly and annual basis.

Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones noted that elevated rates are definitely “deteriorating” the market, and “this month’s deep freeze in buyer activity could persist until affordability improves.”

“The local data confirms that higher rates are impacting buyers throughout the country, even in markets that have shown consistent strength,” she continued.

However, Jones added that even though rates are straining buyer budgets, “the market is becoming more hospitable for those who can afford to participate.”

“Lower prices, a slower pace and more price reductions may help offset some of the impact of higher rates,” she concluded.

The latest Case-Shiller Index saw real home values decline for the 15th straight month as inflation continues to outpace home-price growth.

Home-price growth did see a slight uplift this month, advancing from 1.9% year-over-over growth last month to 2.1% in the latest report. The 10- and 20-City Composites were also both up 0.2% in their annual gains to 3.6% and 2.7%, respectively.

Rebecca Kaufman, associate director of Commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices, did note a discrepancy in seasonally adjusted and non-seasonally adjusted prices (declines vs. rises, respectively), which she explained is indicative of a “post-summer slowdown” that “is obscuring some underlying strength in home prices.”

Kaufman also cautioned that affordability will still face challenges as inflation rises due to gas, oil and energy prices rising.

“Households continue to face elevated costs alongside persistently high home prices,” she said.

As for existing homes, the median existing-home price clocked in at $417,500, which is a 1.3% annual increase. This is a reversal from last month’s 1.2% annual fall, but still a lower rate of growth than historical peaks.

As previously mentioned, housing construction’s challenges have kept the industry segment fairly muted throughout the year, and this month was no expectation.

The latest New Residential Construction report saw housing starts drop 5.2% month-over-month and 7.4% year-over-year, led by 7.2% month-over-month and a whopping 25.9% year-over-year fall in multifamily starts (which had previously been performing well). Single-family starts also remained diminished with a 4.6% fall month-over-month, but did see a slight year-over-year improvement of +2.6%.

Danushka Nanayakkara-Skillington—NAHB’s assistant vice president for forecasting and analysis—noted that this month’s data “align(s) with our forecast of lower production in 2026, with further declines expected in 2027 as rates stay elevated and material costs rise.”

Despite starts remaining diminished, housing completions did see a slight month-over-month uptick by 2.2%. The slight monthly boost is likely due to a 14.9% month-over-month boost in multifamily completions. However, overall completions were still well down year-over-year by 14%, as single-family completions were down across the board and multifamily completions were down year-over-year.

In addition, the fall in multifamily starts may not last for long, as multifamily permits were up 5.9% month-over-month and 1% year-over-year. Overall, permits had the smallest fall in the report, down only 0.2% month-over-month and 3% year-over-year.

“The market is not conducive to building right now, and the diminished starts and completions figures make that clear,” added Realtor.com Senior Economist Joel Berner. “However, the relative resiliency of new home permitting shows that builders see these conditions as temporary.”

With construction reports still coming in well below historical norms, builder confidence remains fairly shaken. The latest Housing Market Index actually saw builder confidence tank to a 14-year low, clocking in at 29 (out of 100, with 50 being the baseline).

The “Trump administration’s efforts to advance regulatory reform” are, according to NAHB Chairman Owens, “helping to ease some of the cost pressures (builders) face.” Nevertheless, the administration’s immigration crackdown is “causing construction delays and discouraging legal workers from reporting to work.”

Price cuts and incentives are still being heavily used by builders to sell new homes, with the share of builders enacting price cuts actually peaking to a six-year high at 43%.

The labor market has seen a lot of resilience in recent months, but this month’s jobs report unfortunately weakened and lost some ground.

The unemployment rate—which has been unchanged at 4.1% for the past two months—saw a slight uptick to 4.2%. Only 29,000 jobs were added this month, which is below economists’ expectations in the range of 80,000.

Realtor.com Senior Economist Jake Krimmel called the report a “clear miss,” but noted that it probably wouldn’t change that much when it came time for the Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting.

“Despite tepid September job growth, unemployment remains low, so in short, this is no labor disaster that would pull the FOMC’s focus off inflation,” he continued.

Krimmel also pointed toward the downward revisions in added jobs over the past two months, explaining that the unemployment rate’s increase is not as severe as people may believe.

“Layoffs haven’t picked up, and jobless claims have been falling, so the low-hire, low-fire market is likely to stay entrenched as we head into 2027,” he said.

Speaking of inflation, the latest Consumer Price Index saw an increase as inflation remains elevated, now clocking in at 3.7% and core inflation at 2.6%. Krimmel noted that these figures “came in slightly hotter than expected,” and potentially point to a Fed rate hike by December.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index also recorded an increase this month, hitting 3.6% annual inflation and 3.1% core annual inflation. Navy Federal Chief Economist Heather Long said that “inflation is back near a 3-year high,” which is “largely due to war in Iran.”

Long also identified other major reasons for inflation—a “(b)ig rise in goods prices,” “service sector inflation” and “sideways” housing inflation as indicative of rising core inflation in general.

The Fed ended up not making any changes to rates, despite many predictions leaning in that direction. However, further rate hikes remain on the table.

Notably, Realtor.com Chief Economist Hale anticipated another two to three hikes over the next six to eight months, which would mean a high-end rate range of 4.5% to 4.75%.

Consumer opinions were slightly mixed this month, as sentiment remained flat while confidence saw an increase.

Sentiment’s lack of movement was largely attributed to the prolonged conflict with Iran. Also, despite little movement this month, sentiment has honed in on a 74-year low in the survey’s history.

Confidence, on the other hand, grew due to growth in positive perceptions of current and expected business conditions. This was attributed to the brief recovery seen in gas prices from September to October. Confidence does, however, remain on the downward trend it has been on over recent years, the report noted.

Looking ahead, the Leading Economic Index registered flat this month as the economy remains challenged due to the aforementioned elevation in inflation. The report was also not indicative of any recession in the coming months.

Claudia Larsen is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5717. Democrats Will Focus on Affordability in 2027, Party Leaders Say

Democrats rode affordability anxieties to big wins in the midterm elections. But they must deliver on lowering costs if they want to sustain their political power, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) said Thursday.

Speaking at a Washington, DC, forum hosted by Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank, Schumer reflected on the significant gains in Tuesday's midterm elections. Democrats were able to flip dozens of seats and gain control of both the House and Senate for the upcoming Congress.

Democrats spent the year attacking President Donald Trump on "costs, chaos, and corruption," as Schumer put it. But although many people voted for Democrats out of frustration with the Trump administration, that doesn't mean they're enthusiastic about the Democratic Party, he conceded.

"We highlighted how Trump's chaos agenda was causing Americans pain at the grocery store, at the gas pump," Schumer said. "Every month in the spring, we focused on the costs of the American people and what we were going to do about it."

Vice President JD Vance has also said that the conflict in Iran and subsequent inflation surge cost Republicans the election. Schumer said Democrats have to bring down costs. Ending the Iran conflict and stopping the tariffs policies that have driven up costs in the country are two ways to do that.

Although Democrats made major gains, they still won't have enough votes to override a Trump veto. And Democratic leadership will have to find common ground with the party's left flank after a wave of Democratic Socialist candidates won elections on Tuesday, a fact Schumer acknowledged without mentioning the group by name.

"Unity means linking arms with people you will not agree with on every issue so you can make progress on the more important areas where you agree," Schumer said. "Intra-party debate isn't a sign of weakness."

Democrats who won state and local races have promised affordability-minded reforms and emphasized housing production. That's crucial in expensive areas such as California and Washington DC.

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker said at the CAP event that medical and student debt are also issues Democrats should tackle at the federal level. These debts significantly delay homeownership. But he said both oversight and affordability should be Congress' main focus next year.

"You can walk and chew gum, we have to deal with affordability, that has to be the principal thing," Pritzer said. "But we have to have oversight committees, just like the Republicans did."

On Wednesday, New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, who is likely to become the new speaker of the House, said the House Democratic Caucus will convene next week and lay out an agenda. But Democrats would focus on "affordability and accountability" with their new majority, he said.

Democrats after the election threw out a host of ideas for items to pursue in 2027 and 2028. Many of them focused on both affordability and guardrails for artificial intelligence and data centers.

"Top of the Democratic agenda on day 1 needs to be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of this out of control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence," Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-AZ) posted to X on Wednesday.

The Nasdaq plunged 5% the next day, led by a sharp decline in tech stocks.

Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT), who caucuses with the Democrats, called for a national 5% wealth tax in a video message Thursday morning. Such a tax, as is being considered in California, could fund 7 million units of affordable housing, Sanders said.

Realtor.com® economists quantified just how bad the affordability situation is for Americans.

In January, a $2,000 monthly mortgage payment supported a home price $28,500 higher than a year earlier. By October 2026, that same payment supported a home price $33,600 lower. The surge in interest rates, from 6.05% in February to 7.33% in October, was to blame for the $62,100 swing.

“Mortgage rates are not abstract to a family trying to buy a home,” says Danielle Hale, chief economist at Realtor.com. “They show up as the home they can no longer afford."

"The year-over-year comparison is a vivid measure of why housing affordability lands as a pocketbook issue for voters," Hale continues. "The conflict’s inflationary impact is one source of uncertainty, but households feel the consequences in their monthly budgets and in the homes they have to take off their list.”

In a post, National Association of Homebuilders Chief Advocacy Officer Ken Wingert urged the next Congress to craft more housing bills like the comprehensive 21st Century Road to Housing Act that passed this summer.

Lawmakers have suggested they have their own sets of ideas for new housing measures to pursue. Cities and localities, they have said, must also step up to implement new laws.

Those rules must assuage builders whose confidence has been shattered by high costs of building materials and high mortgage rates chasing homebuyers out of the market. The National Association of Home Builders/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) fell to a 14-year low last month.

"With a national housing shortfall of roughly 1.2 million households, more must be done to let builders build—and voters agree," Wingert said. "Throughout the campaign, voters consistently cited housing availability and affordability as key factors in their decisions."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5716. 5 Packing Tips for a Smooth Move

Moving can be a time-consuming process, but it doesn't need to be stressful. We have some tips to help you enjoy a smooth move from your old home to the new. With the right system in place, there is no need to be overwhelmed by the move.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:

Greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert says, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the new place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need."

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. Instead, pack a suitcase with a few days' worth of clothes and necessities for everyone in the house. This way, you can settle into your new home without scrambling to find a towel or toothbrush before spending your first night there.

The suitcase should include more than just your change of clothes and toiletries. Anything you might need for 2-3 days should be packed in it, including:

As you pack, or have your movers pack, label each box with not just the contents inside but the room it should be placed in at the new home. This way, whether you have professional movers, a team of friends and family, or just your own household, it will be easy to make sure each box lands in the proper place.

One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. All boxes that should be brought to the kitchen will be labeled with blue tape, and on move-in day you can hang a large blue paper in the kitchen. This simple system will make unpacking much smoother.

#5713. Los Angeles Mayor-Elect Nithya Raman Vows To Triple Homebuilding To Improve Affordability

Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman has unseated the city's Democrat incumbent Mayor Karen Bass after running a campaign centered on affordability and housing.

The Associated Press called the election for Raman on Thursday afternoon as she widened her lead over Bass.

Bass, 73, called Raman to concede her loss and congratulate her successor on her victory.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken," the outgoing mayor said in a statement. "I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition. Moving this city forward is what Los Angeles needs from all of us."

The win underscored a "blue wave" that swept Democrats into control of both chambers of Congress, delivering a decisive rebuke to President Donald Trump and the Republican Party.

When Raman, 45, takes office in January, L.A. will become the nation's second-largest city led by a Democratic Socialist, following in the footsteps of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

Raman's swearing-in will expand a growing roster of Democratic Socialist mayors nationwide, including Janeese Lewis George in Washington, DC, Katie Wilson in Seattle, and David Morales in Providence, RI.

Ahead of her victory, Raman appeared before a jubilant crowd of supporters at the Greek Theatre Plaza in Griffith Park on Tuesday, arguing that L.A. voters were frustrated with Bass' record on the cost of living and were demanding change, reported KTLA5.

"We watched friend after friend, family after family, leave because they couldn’t afford to stay here anymore. And we all talked about it as if these things were completely out of City Hall’s control," she told the audience. "That’s the cynicism that started to take over this city. That started to make us believe that L.A.’s problems weren't just bad, but they were permanent."

Raman ran a campaign focusing on housing, homelessness, and safety issues. The centerpiece of her platform was a plan to triple annual housing production by speeding up permitting through strict "shot clocks" for approvals.

Further proposals included overhauling inspections, updating codes, and eliminating additional fees to incentivize developers to build more starter homes.

"Today, less than 10% of the new homes built in L.A. are for sale," Raman recently told Realtor.com®. "Under current city and state regulations, for-sale projects are charged higher fees, have a more complicated approval process, are easier to appeal, and have increased liability risks for developers."

The councilmember was sharply critical of her mayoral predecessor, contending that Bass has not done enough to tackle L.A.’s yearslong housing crisis.

Bass’ record includes signing Executive Directive 1, which streamlined approval for roughly 50,000 units of fully affordable housing, overseeing a historic rezoning program to clear a path for building a half-million new homes, adding more housing units to transit corridors and job hubs, simplifying the building application process, and updating rent stabilization rules for the first time in 40 years to shield tenants from steep hikes.

However, it was on Bass’ watch that the Realtor.com Metro Report Cards released in September ranked L.A. the nation’s least affordable large city—a result that Raman did not find surprising.

"We’ve made it too difficult, time-consuming, and costly to build homes in Los Angeles," concluded Raman.

Assuming a 10% down payment and a 6.5% 30-year fixed mortgage, a median earner in L.A. would have to spend nearly 85% of their income on monthly mortgage payments on a $1.12 million median-priced home, effectively putting ownership out of reach of all but the wealthiest buyers.

Beyond cost-of-living issues, Raman faces pressure upon taking office to deliver on her lofty campaign pledge to reduce citywide homelessness by 50% in time for the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles.

Fulfilling that promise will be a major challenge, given that recent 2026 data showed roughly 45,000 people living in tents and encampments on the streets of L.A.

#5712. SmartMLS Introduces New Ownership Verification Tool to Help Combat Seller-Impersonation and Land Scams

With security and insurance symbols prominently featured, the property house cautioned against falling victim to scammers and fraud.

Connecticut’s SmartMLS has announced that it will introduce a new Ownership Verification tool from Property Shield designed to help real estate professionals combat seller-impersonation and vacant-land scams.

According to a release, the new technology, expected to become available to SmartMLS next week, provides an additional way for real estate professionals to verify the identity of someone claiming to own a property before accepting a listing.

Seller-impersonation fraud typically begins when a scammer poses as a property owner and contacts a real estate professional seeking to list and sell property the scammer does not own. These schemes can be particularly difficult to identify when the property is vacant land or when the purported seller communicates remotely.

“Seller-impersonation scams can be difficult to identify.” said Kathy Elson, CEO of SmartMLS. “We want to give our users a tool to help verify a prospective seller’s identity and identify a potential problem as early in the listing process as possible.”

An additional step when something doesn’t look right

Property Shield’s Ownership Verification tool is designed to help determine whether the individual claiming to be the property owner is who they say they are.

The verification process uses identity verification and facial-recognition technology in conjunction with property ownership information to provide an additional layer of protection when questions arise about the identity of a prospective seller.

Rather than relying solely on documents, emails, telephone conversations, or information supplied by the prospective seller, real estate professionals will have a tool available to help evaluate whether the person attempting to list the property is legitimate.

“Real estate professionals are often on the front line when seller-impersonation fraud is attempted,” Elson said. “The challenge is that a sophisticated scammer may have enough information about the property and its owner to appear legitimate. Ownership Verification gives our users another way to ask an important question before proceeding: Is this really the property owner?”

Helping stop fraud before a listing enters the MLS

Ownership Verification complements the Listing Fraud Protection technology SmartMLS has already introduced through its partnership with Property Shield.

The two technologies address fraud at different points.

Listing Fraud Protection helps identify when legitimate SmartMLS listing information is copied and used in potentially fraudulent advertisements across the web.

Ownership Verification is designed to help identify potential seller impersonation before a fraudulent listing enters the MLS.

Together, the tools provide SmartMLS users with additional ways to identify and respond to real estate fraud.

“Seller impersonation and vacant-land fraud are difficult problems because the person committing the fraud may never meet the agent face-to-face,” said Alexander Fahsel, CEO of Property Shield. “Ownership Verification gives real estate professionals another layer of information to help determine whether the person they are dealing with is actually connected to the property they are attempting to sell.”

Technology supporting professional judgment

Ownership Verification is intended to provide an additional fraud-prevention tool, not replace the judgment and due diligence of the real estate professional.

A successful verification should not eliminate other appropriate steps when circumstances surrounding a prospective listing raise concerns. Similarly, an issue identified during verification can provide an important signal that additional investigation may be warranted before proceeding with the listing.

“Our goal isn’t to replace the due diligence brokers and agents already perform,” Elson said. “It’s to give them a better tool when they need it. If something about a prospective seller or listing doesn’t add up, we want our users to have another way to investigate before moving forward.”

For more information, visit smartmls.com and propertyshield.co.

Flay, 61, dropped another helpful piece of advice: “Have chicken stock on your stove. It reheats the sliced turkey, which ultimately gets dried out no matter what you do. It can also thin out gravy that gets too thick.”

The kitchen of the Amagansett home is his favorite place to cook and where he has typically hosted Thanksgiving.

#5710. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5709. Texas Man Admits to $1.5 Million Deed Fraud Scheme Involving Properties in 4 States

An empty piece of land might seem like an easy real estate investment opportunity, but for unsuspecting property owners across the country, those plots of land became targets in an alleged $1.5 million deed fraud scheme carried out by four men posing as the landowners.

Moshe Levi, 61, of Carrollton, TX, has admitted to helping carry out the plan, which involved impersonating property owners, arranging fraudulent sales, and laundering the proceeds, federal prosecutors announced this week.

On Wednesday, Levi pleaded guilty in a Boston federal courtroom to conspiracy to commit wire fraud and conspiracy to commit money laundering. The fraudulent property sales totaled more than $1.5 million, according to prosecutors.

Levi was one of three people indicted in July 2026. According to court filings, Levi and his alleged co-conspirators targeted vacant, unencumbered properties in Massachusetts, Georgia, Indiana, and Tennessee.

“Mr. Levi deeply regrets his conduct,” Levi's attorney, Ian Gold, tells Realtor.com®. “The plea represents an important step toward accountability to the victims and society.”

The scheme hit home for Halla Shami Jaraki, who owns a vacant lot on Mattison Drive in Concord, MA, but lives in South Carolina with her husband, Omar.

The couple had hoped to return to Massachusetts or pass the land along to one of their sons. Instead, their property was sold in 2024 for roughly $525,000 by someone allegedly posing as the owner, according to The Concord Bridge.

Developers began to build on the property but were stopped when the couple obtained an injunction against them. According to prosecutors, this couple’s experience was how the scheme worked.

Levi and his co-conspirators targeted vacant properties owned by people who lived out of state, then created email and internet-based phone accounts in the owners' names. They also obtained fake driver’s licenses and passports with the names of the property owners.

The group then used the forged documents and accounts to impersonate the owners of the properties and then allegedly persuaded real estate agents to list the properties, negotiate the sale of the properties, and transfer the deed to the unsuspecting buyer for payment.

The scheme allegedly extended beyond the fraudulent sales. Prosecutors said Levi and his co-conspirators moved money through individual and corporate bank accounts they controlled, using checks and wire transfers to conceal the source, ownership, and control of the proceeds.

Since around June 2023, Levi and others have shared or attempted to share in approximately $1 million in illegal proceeds, prosecutors said.

In April 2025, the FBI’s Boston office warned of an increase in deed fraud cases, with the rise of remote real estate transactions providing opportunities for “title pirates.” Property owners are being urged to be on the lookout for a number of warning signs, including missing property tax and water bills and sudden and unexplained increases in utility charges at vacant properties.

In a survey released in September from the American Land Title Association, 59% of title firms reported at least one incident of seller impersonation fraud in the prior year, which is more than double the 28% reported in the 2024 survey.

Levi will be sentenced on Feb. 11, 2027. He faces up to 20 years on each of the two counts of conspiracy to commit wire fraud.

Prosecutors said they would recommend prison time “at the low end” of the sentencing guidelines, along with a fine “at the low end” of the guidelines, three years of supervised release, forfeiture, and at least $1.34 million in restitution.

Levi was charged along with Kyon James of Middleborough, MA, and Bradley Beauge of Somerset, NJ. Those charges for money laundering conspiracy are currently pending.

A fourth co-conspirator is based in Nigeria, but prosecutors have not publicly released their name.

#5707. EXCLUSIVE: Ryan Serhant Warns Homebuyers Against Waiting for 2027: ‘You Don’t Want to Wait Until It’s Too Late’

Ryan Serhant is warning would-be homebuyers against assuming that lower mortgage rates will deliver an easier path to homeownership in 2027—and says the housing market has a problem that cheaper borrowing alone cannot solve.

Speaking exclusively to Realtor.com®, Serhant shared his outlook for the year ahead, identified markets he believes could surprise buyers, and weighed in on the debate over private listings.

He also offered a glimpse inside his own townhouse and revealed a buyer request that has him searching for an enormous stretch of land with its own airport.

At the center of his housing outlook is a concern about people at opposite ends of the property ladder being unable to move.

“We have entered an environment where people can't afford to buy their first home, and their parents can't afford to leave their last one, and it's a problem we need to solve," he said.

“Lower mortgage rates will help, but rates alone are not going to fix the cost of housing or the cost of moving. We need to create more supply and fewer obstacles," Serhant added.

Serhant argued that the system has become an obstacle to moving, with consequences that have developed over many years.

“I think that what we've created is a environment, that is punishing mobility. Instead of rewarding mobility. And this was set up a long, long time ago. We didn't get here overnight.”

“Like, the housing market and the system we operate in rewards stability, because what's… it makes everyone feel comfortable. But then when that stability does not move, because stability is stability, mobility is mobility. Then everyone gets angry, and that's the environment that we're currently in.”

For his outlook, he is watching whether households have both the confidence and the resources to act.

“I think I'm watching employment, and I'm watching household confidence right now. I think pent-up demand only becomes a transaction when people have the confidence and the financial ability to act, and we'll see if that happens anytime soon.”

For people who can afford to buy but are considering waiting for a better deal in 2027, Serhant pointed to opportunities he believes already exist.

“I think in a lot of markets, we've entered a buyer's market now. You have the ability to negotiate in markets that you haven't been able to negotiate in in the past couple years.”

“I think there's a great opportunity to use the rate pressure that we have to negotiate closing costs, to negotiate rate buy-downs, to negotiate lower purchase prices, to get a house that really, really, really works for you. Remember, it is such an old and annoying saying, but you do marry the house, and you do date through the rates.”

His argument rests on the potential trade-off between borrowing costs and competition, although his comments about future rates and inventory are predictions.

“The market does become very stagnant. Interest rates should come down, and remember, you can refinance. And you should use the opportunity right now, if you can afford it, to purchase in a high-interest rate environment, because there's less competition.”

“Everyone wants low rates, they never want what comes with it. You know what'll happen if rates come down? There will be no houses for sale.”

“You won't even have the opportunity to complain about a high monthly payment. You won't even be able to talk about—the lack of affordability. You won't be able to complain, because there will be nothing for sale, because the demand is so great. There is not nearly enough houses for the demand we have in this country. Every 40-year-old who still lives at home will then move.”

Serhant also argued that the circumstances accompanying lower rates can make buyers reluctant to purchase.

“And what also brings down low interest rates is job insecurity. You know, is unemployment, is war. Are things that happen in the global environment that will make people, not confident to go and make a massive purchase. And so, you might miss that opportunity, too.”

He used the early months of the pandemic to illustrate his point about confidence and timing.

“In the spring of 2020, that was a great time to buy. But no, we had COVID, 'You can't buy. There's a death ticker on the bottom of every TV screen. You might not live.' You didn't take advantage of this environment, and then when the market came back, it was too late.”

“And so, I would use this moment to move quickly, because when things do even out, and they always do, markets go up and markets go down. Always. And forever. You don't want to wait until it's too late.”

Serhant highlighted returning city residents and investment in jobs as themes behind his market picks.

“I think people are returning to cities in a way that we haven't seen before. It's one of the reasons we just were launching, officially Chicago. This coming Wednesday. I'm incredibly excited about that.”

“The demand and the volume we've seen from all of our other Serhant markets wanting to move back to Chicago, who moved out over the past couple years. Taking advantage of good value, like we just talked about, is really exciting.”

“And I think places where you're seeing incredible job growth. Areas like Ohio, where there's major, major tech investment, not just in data centers. In office. And in manufacturing.”

“We have a lot of investment that's going into Western Pennsylvania, and, you're also seeing a lot of movement into Alabama.”

“You know, I think there are markets that will really, really surprise you because of great quality of life for the best cost structure the country has to offer.”

Away from the business of buying and selling, Serhant shared the first thing he does when he walks into his townhouse.

“I yell out my daughter's name. I wanted to see where she is in my house. We have a townhouse, so I'm trying to figure out which floor she's on, so I can, you know, prepare.”

His favorite spaces include a gym on the lower level, although his affection extends to the whole property.

“I have a pretty awesome gym. In the lower level that I built out, that's really, really cool, and I think that's pretty awesome, but I mean, I built it with my bare hand. It was a TV show that we did for Bravo about our renovation, and I love that house. Whole thing is great.”

He also described the practical details that help make his kitchen work, starting with a concealed ladder for reaching high cabinets.

“We have incredibly high ceilings. So we have a hidden ladder in our kitchen that looks like the baseboard under the kitchen. Island, and it pops out with the touch of your toe.”

“And, the ladder shows up, and so for anyone, you know, you know, who's vertically challenged to be able to reach upper cabinetry without having a ladder in front of your face at all times, so that you can still enjoy all that light and sunshine and high ceilings, I think is key.”

“Probably the greatest things that we have also in that kitchen are touchless, so, like, the sink, you know, you're cooking, and your hands are messy, and you're always hitting the thing. We have the kitchen sink, where all you have to do is tap it, and it turns on.”

“And so you just hit it with the back of your hand, and it turns on. So you're not, like, also getting the sink and the faucet dirty.”

“And then the same thing for the kitchen refrigerator and freezer. All you do is you slowly kind of, like, tap it with your elbow, or with the side, so you're not, like, yanking on anything, and it automatically just reveals itself to you. I think those little touches are overlooked.”

Among the unusual requests Serhant receives, one current search involves a vast amount of land—and a private airport.

“They're all wild. I'm dealing with somebody right now that wants 100,000 acres of land, which is impossible, for the most part."

For all the features a buyer might want, Serhant has one clear priority when choosing a home.

“You can change everything about the house you want over the years, you can grow into it, you can grow out of it, you can update it, you can paint it, you can flip it upside down. Unless you are Ken Griffin, and you can pick up a house, and you can move it, for the most part. Change the location.”

“And so, you always buy location first. Whatever that is, wherever that place is you want to be for the next 5-10 years, and most times you're paying more. But no one ever paid too much. And regretted it years later. Very, very rarely does that happen.”

“Remember, if you buy a trophy, you get to sell a trophy. If you buy a discount, because you're cheap, you will have to sell a discount. And you will feel cheap.”
