#5706. The chips are down: Qualcomm falls on revenue miss, weak guidance; Arm and GlobalFoundries do little better

Chipmakers Qualcomm Inc., Arm Holdings Ltd. and GlobalFoundries Ltd. struggled to move the needle today after reporting financial results that clearly left investors wanting more.

After an impressive earnings beat from Advanced Micro Devices Inc. just 24 hours earlier, investors may have had heightened expectations. But if they did, on a day when the market rocketed higher on the U.S. election results, they were clearly let down by the shaky performance of Qualcomm, which beat expectations on earnings but missed on revenue and offered weak guidance. The result was predictable, with its stock down more than 6% after-hours.

Both Arm and GlobalFoundries did better, but it wasn’t enough to satisfy investors who are becoming increasingly concerned about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence industry that has driven significant growth for all three chipmakers over the last couple of years.

The biggest disappointment was Qualcomm, which reported fourth-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.17 per share on revenue of $10.44 billion, up just 8% from a year earlier. The results were mixed, with Wall Street looking for earnings of $2.16 per share on sales of $10.48 billion. For the current quarter, Qualcomm said it’s looking for earnings of around $2.25 per share at the midpoint of its guidance range on sales of $10.48 billion, falling short of the Street’s target of $2.27 per share in earnings and $10.48 billion in revenue.

Qualcomm’s troubles stem from the fact that it has less exposure to the AI industry’s rampant growth than many other chipmakers. The bulk of its sales comes from system-on-chips and modems for smartphones. But the market is currently reeling due to the rising cost of components such as memory, which have forced handset makers to bump up their prices, reducing demand. Qualcomm has tried to weather the storm by raising the prices of its own chips recently, but its smartphone chip sales fell 26% in the quarter to just $5.14 billion, well behind the Street’s target of $5.21 billion.

Under Chief Executive Cristiano Amon (pictured), Qualcomm has tried to pivot and grow its position in alternative chip markets, particularly the AI data center industry. Revenue from that segment rose to $650 million during the quarter, but it’s still dwarfed by the smartphone business.

Nonetheless, Amon insisted that the company will grow its data center business to more than $5 billion in revenue by the end of fiscal 2027. He said the company recently struck a deal with an unnamed global hyperscaler for optical connectivity chips. “We don’t have a demand issue; it’s a supply issue,” he told analysts on a conference call. “If I had more supply, I would probably be doing better.”

Qualcomm’s automotive business was a bright spot, with sales there rising 89% to $1.99 billion in the quarter, above the Street’s consensus estimate of $1.66 billion. Internet of Things revenue came to $1.88 billion, up 4% from a year ago and just ahead of the Street’s estimate.

Finally, there’s Qualcomm’s QTL business, which generates revenue from licensing intellectual property for modems, 5G connectivity and other technologies. That segment added $1.3 billion in revenue, down 7%, despite signing renewed licensing agreements with Apple Inc., Transsion Inc. and Huawei Technologies Co. Ltd.

Chip design company Arm delivered much more palatable results, but it was somewhat cautious with its guidance for the current quarter, and its stock was down 2% in late trading today. The company reported adjusted earnings of 52 cents per share, just beating the Street’s target of 48 cents, while revenue rose 27% from a year earlier, to $1.44 billion, ahead of the $1.38 billion analyst estimate.

Unlike Qualcomm, Arm doesn’t manufacture complete chips for its customers, but instead designs and licenses processor blueprints for customers such as Apple Inc., Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. and Qualcomm to build their own custom chips. Where Arm is more similar to Qualcomm is in its strategy, where it too is also pivoting to focus on data center chip designs, trying to tap into the demand for AI compute. Arm said its data center business was the main growth driver this year, with royalties there doubling year-over-year.

However, Arm’s guidance did little to excite investors. The company said it’s looking for earnings of 56 cents per share, plus or minus four cents, compared with Wall Street’s forecast of 55 cents per share. For revenue, it’s targeting $1.54 billion, plus or minus $50 million, which is just ahead of the Street’s $1.52 billion target.

GlobalFoundries did a little better than its peers today, posting results and guidance for the current that squeaked past expectations. However, its stock remained flat after-hours.

The company reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of 53 cents per share on sales of $1.9 billion, up 12% from a year earlier, with growth driven by strong demand from AI and data center customers, it said. The results were better than expected, with analysts targeting earnings of 51 cents on revenue of $1.89 billion.

GlobalFoundries’ also differs from Qualcomm, in that it’s a pure-play contract manufacturer that builds the processors designed by semiconductors firms, rather than designing chips itself or selling them under its own brand. Qualcomm is actually one of its biggest customers, alongside Broadcom Inc., NXP Semiconductors N.V. and Infineon Technologies Inc. As such, its fortunes are very much aligned with those of the chip designers it caters too.

For the current quarter, GlobalFoundries said it’s looking for earnings of 59 cents per share, plus or minus five cents, on revenue of about $2 billion. Wall Street is looking for earnings of 57 cents per share and has the same revenue target.

#5705. French blood banks hacked amid ‘deeply concerning’ wave of fridge and freezer cyberattacks in Europe

In a recent spate of cyberattacks in Europe against fridges and freezers, the latest assault hit France’s national blood service, where hackers gained control of cold storage systems at medical facilities and turned up the temperature.

The French Blood Establishment, EFS, told media that the facilities managed to save the blood supplies and there has been “no loss of blood products.” But the attacks come after supermarkets in several European countries experienced hacks of their fridges and freezers leading to the loss of millions of Euros in products.

Last month, hackers hit hundreds of supermarkets across France where temperatures were forced up to 50 degrees C overnight in what officials called an “unprecedented” attack. Food losses and fires were reported after “connected refrigerators ⁠in several ​major food retailers across France.” What followed was a wave of similar attacks across the continent where fridges and freezers at stores in the U.K., Italy and Germany were recently hacked, following attacks in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Finland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden.

“They are a deliberate attempt to disrupt our food supply chain and undermine ​consumers’ confidence in it – a warning that we must take seriously,” said EU Commissioner for Agriculture Christophe Hansen. “The repeated occurrence of these cyberattacks is deeply concerning.”

Connected fridges can now be controlled and monitored remotely through internet-connected software but with this comes vulnerabilities. Hackers can exploit publicly reachable, legacy or unpatched remote refrigeration management controllers that may use default passwords or weak date-based administrative bypasses.

“Retail is an easy target because retail chains run enormous estates of refrigeration controllers, building management systems, door access panels and point-of-sale gear,” Tom Hegel of the cybersecurity firm SentinelOne, told Reuters.

Cybersecurity experts so far have not figured out who’s behind the attacks. Russian hacking groups are a possibility as well as Iranian hacktivists or nation-state hackers. It might also be kids pulling off what have so far been very expensive pranks. Cybersecurity researchers at some firms have installed fake software as honeypots in an attempt to gather information about the hackers.

#5704. An 18th-Century Connecticut Estate With ‘Little Women’ Ties Lists for $1.5 Million—Hidden Treasures Included

An 18th-century antique home in Wolcott, CT, with ties to a famous clockmaker and the Trans-Siberian Orchestra just hit the market for $1.5 million.

Listed for the first time in decades, the 1.94-acre property known as Spindle Hill includes a 5,360-square-foot primary residence, a hand-hewn barn, a manor home, an a history of treasure-filled walls.

"When you walk into the original section of the home, you feel the history," says listing agent Donna Membrino of William Pitt Sotheby’s International Realty. "The keeping room has an original beehive oven and a wooden mantel."

The property’s origins date to the early 1700s, when the land was purchased by the town’s first settler, the patriarch of the Alcott family, according to Membrino. Nathaniel Lane and Millicent Alcott Lane, the uncle and aunt of "Little Women" author Louisa May Alcott, later developed it into a working farm that stayed in the Lane family for generations.

The property is also linked to famed clockmaker Seth Thomas, who launched his first clockmaking venture from his childhood home just down the road.

“It was very important to the seller to preserve the home’s history, and they have taken great pains to do that,” Membrino says.

Marlene Tosun, who grew up on Spindle Hill Farm, became the owner of the property in the 1950s.

After moving in, she uncovered a series of hidden treasures: a violin beneath the floorboards of the main house; Nathaniel Lane’s diary, containing his handwritten business accounts, tucked behind a wall; and tomahawk heads embedded in the estate’s original hand-stacked stone walls, which are believed to have been built by Native Americans.

Membrino said the family also discovered a pair of 1700s wheels from Lane’s ox-drawn wagon, which was used to deliver goods to early New England customers.

The seller, Marlene’s daughter Sylvia Tosun, was once the lead vocalist for the Trans-Siberian Orchestra. She also featured on an international EDM hit championed by DJ Armin van Buuren.

In a meticulous restoration, Tosun set out to preserve the property’s original charm and character while bringing it up to modern luxury standards.

Original weathered wood salvaged from older, dismantled sections of the house was used to detail the Grand Salon. Other highlights include a black-and-white marble foyer, a 50-foot turret with an antique Schonbek chandelier, double-height cathedral ceilings, reclaimed wide-plank heart pine floors, a handcarved Italian marble chimneypiece, and three wood-burning fireplaces.

A modernized kitchen with Shaker cabinetry and granite countertops flows into a sunny dining room. Upstairs, the primary suite has a private terrace. The walk-out garden level features a wet bar and a “grand fireplace lounge” that serves as a professional recording studio.

The property also offers twin gazebos, a sunken patio, fruit trees and vegetable gardens, as well as “rare legal multi-family zoning” that allows for three private dwellings.

“Wolcott is a great town,” Membrino adds. “It’s close to Waterbury and Hartford but has more of a country feel, and it’s centrally located between New York and Boston.”

Buyers should note that “the antique barn is being sold in as-is condition,” according to the listing.

Kellie Speed is a contributor to Realtor.com. #5703. Kyndryl shares surge 30% on hyperscaler-related revenue growth

Shares of Kyndryl Holdings Inc. jumped 30% today after it reported better-than-expected earnings for the second quarter of its 2027 fiscal year.

Kyndryl generated $3.9 billion in sales during the three months ended Sept. 30. That represents a 1.9% decrease from a year earlier, but the company still managed to top the consensus estimate by about $50 million. It attributed the top-line surprise to its Kyndryl Consult business.

Kyndryl, a former IBM Corp. unit, once generated nearly all its revenue from managing other companies’ technology infrastructure. In 2022, it launched Kyndryl Consult to take on more strategic, higher-margin professional services deals.

The unit’s revenue grew 4.2% year-over-year in the second quarter. Kyndryl didn’t share a specific quarterly revenue number, but divulged that the unit earned a total of $3.6 billion over the past 12 months.

Kyndryl Consult’s signings, a measure of future revenue, jumped 19% over the past year. That momentum may have contributed to the company’s stock rally today.

Many of the projects that Kyndryl Consult takes on involve artificial intelligence. The unit can help customers build AI agent ensembles and set up training data generation pipelines. Additionally, it can advise clients about business decisions such as how they should allocate their AI budgets.

Kyndryl offers a software platform called Bridge to companies that buy its AI services. It enables AI agents to access business data from an organization’s internal systems. Additionally, Bridge monitors those agents to ensure they adhere to safety requirements.

The public cloud is another major focus of Kyndryl’s growth efforts. The company’s hyperscale-related revenue topped $500 million in the second quarter, which amounts to a 27% year-over-year increase.

“Strong signings and continued growth in Kyndryl Consult and hyperscaler-related revenue reinforce our confidence in our fiscal 2027 outlook,” said Kyndryl Chief Executive Officer Martin Schroeter. “Our performance reflects demand for Kyndryl’s AI-led modernization capabilities and deep mission-critical expertise that help customers evolve their complex technology environments, strengthen cybersecurity and achieve measurable business outcomes.”

The company delivered an adjusted net income of $92 million, which breaks down to 42 cents per share. Analysts expected 41 cents per share. The sum excludes a $38 million workforce reduction charge the company took in the second quarter. It’s part of a broader cost-cutting initiative that is set to save up to $500 million annually starting from Kyndryl’s 2028 fiscal year.

For the current fiscal year, the company is forecasting an adjusted pretax income of $600 million to $700 million. Kyndryl expects its revenue to be flat or increase by up to 2%.

#5702. ‘It’s H for Housing’: How Texas Democrats Plan To Build on GOP Homebuilding Momentum

Texas enacted some of its most consequential housing supply reforms in years under Republican leadership, but Tuesday's historic Democratic sweep in the Lone Star State has suddenly opened the door to changes advocates thought were politically impossible.

“The boundaries shifted entirely for the possibilities for low-income households and Texans seeking affordability,” Texas Housers, a nonprofit housing advocacy organization, tells Realtor.com®. "What was realistic 24 hours ago is dramatically different from what is realistic today.”

Among those possibilities are greater state investment in affordable housing, stronger renter protections, and more funding to rebuild homes damaged by natural disasters—priorities the organization hopes the incoming administration will advance.

But the state's homebuilding industry is looking to build on an agenda it has spent years advancing with officials from both parties.

"It's neither D nor R. It's H for housing," Scott Norman, CEO of the Texas Association of Builders, tells Realtor.com.

After an election shaped by pocketbook concerns, Texas' new guard will doubtless be judged on whether it can solve for Norman's 'H'—turning the momentum of the nation's most active homebuilding market into homes more Texans can afford.

Texas' Republican-led Legislature had already begun dismantling barriers to housing construction before Tuesday's election.

Senate Bill 840, for example, allows developers to convert certain commercial properties into apartments without extensive rezoning.

Since taking effect in September 2025, the law has enabled plans for at least 8,400 apartments, according to a July analysis by the Texas Tribune citing a coalition of housing reform advocates. That's equivalent to roughly one-fifth of the multifamily units permitted statewide during the period.

That’s an especially notable share given that the Lone Star State leads the nation in homebuilding, issuing more permits than any other state and accounting for 14.6% of building permits issued nationwide, according to the latest Affordability and Homebuilding Report Cards from Realtor.com.

But to Norman's point, it was a bipartisan push—one that Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa helped advance during her time in the state Legislature. As a member of the House Land & Resource Management Committee, she voted in favor of moving SB 840 forward.

It's something Norman hasn’t forgotten, saying she was "supportive of stuff we were pushing" during the previous legislative session. "I'm sure and I know she'll take that experience to the governor's mansion.”

Tray Bates, vice president of governmental affairs at Texas Realtors, also sees room for cooperation.

"The core problem is supply," Bates tells Realtor.com. "Texas is adding people faster than it's adding homes people can afford."

Both organizations want to continue easing restrictions on residential development, while Norman also sees an opportunity to address the shortage of skilled construction workers through expanded workforce training.

"The more folks we can get in the business, that'll drive down those labor costs," he says.

But Texas' homebuilding boom has done far less to close the gap for its lowest-income renters.

The state faces a shortage of 709,000 affordable and available rentals for extremely low-income households, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition.

Texas Housers argues that insufficient state investment has contributed to that shortfall.

"Texas has relied almost entirely on federal dollars and tax credits to create and preserve affordable housing in our communities," the organization says. "Current resources are not enough to address the need for safe, decent, and affordable housing."

Indeed, just $10.1 million in state funding was allocated to the Housing Trust Fund for fiscal years 2026 and 2027. By contrast, the state awarded more than $114 million in federal housing tax credits to help finance affordable rental units in 2026 alone.

The programs serve different purposes, to be sure, but the figures illustrate how heavily Texas relies on federal incentives to finance affordable rental development.

Land Commissioner-elect Ben Flores sees another opportunity in the approximately 13 million acres managed by the General Land Office.

"We [sic] hold parcels near growing cities that are sitting idle," Flores tells Realtor.com. "My team will inventory those parcels and identify which ones could support housing for teachers, nurses, first responders, and working families through long-term leases that keep the land in public hands and still earn revenue for the Permanent School Fund.

"Housing and school funding don't have to compete," he adds. "Done right, they support each other."

Flores intends to prioritize the Houston region and Rio Grande Valley, where he says rising housing costs have compounded the challenges facing families recovering from floods.

He's also promising to address delays in distributing disaster recovery aid—an issue Texas Housers says has left some Hurricane Harvey survivors waiting years to rebuild.

"When the state relies solely on federal dollars run through slow, unaccountable systems, the families with the least end up waiting the longest," the organization says.

Flores says he'll tackle this head-on in his first 90 days by conducting an agency audit, with public progress reports every 30 days and measurable targets for distributing assistance.

"We will review every open recovery program, find out where funds are stuck and why, and work to get those dollars back to hurricane survivors," Flores says. "Allocation decisions will be made based on need and damage, not politics, and we'll publish where the money is going so Texans can see it for themselves."

Renters could also see a different approach under the incoming administration.

"Basic tenant protections are also urgently needed," Texas Housers says, calling for eviction record sealing and greater transparency around rental fees among its legislative priorities.

Lt. Gov.-elect Vikki Goodwin has proposed property tax incentives for landlords who maintain affordable rents, while Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson has promised a 30-day review of consumer protection and competition laws, specifically identifying algorithmic rent-setting as an enforcement concern.

Then there are the forces outside what any single public office can control—forces that Norman argues will be the greater determinants of Texas' housing future.

"Two things that drive housing growth are population growth and job growth," he says.

And there’s been no shortage of that in Texas. The state has added more than 2.6 million residents since 2020, according to U.S. Census Bureau figures.

When asked about fears that growth could stall or reverse, Norman responds with enthusiastic optimism that the state's economic appeal will continue attracting households and supporting construction.

But some real estate professionals outside the state are watching for signs that the political shift could change where affluent residents choose to live.

Miltiadis Kastanis, a Miami Beach luxury real estate agent with Compass, says inquiries from Texas buyers were rising before the election.

"We have noticed an increase in inquiries from the Texan market," he says.

Kastanis believes the latest political shifts could accelerate that interest, particularly among wealthy Texans concerned about future changes to the state's tax environment.

"You will see Texans start pre-planning a move to the Florida market," he says, but he cautions against expecting a mass exodus or COVID-19 pandemic-era bidding wars.

Bates is similarly skeptical that one election will significantly alter migration patterns.

"It's far too early to predict migration based on one election," he says. "Domestic migration to Texas was already slowing before Tuesday, and housing costs are a major factor."

And at a crossroads for Texas housing policy, that could become a North Star for housing advocates, industry leaders, and the incoming administration alike.

"Maybe the policy solutions may look a little different based on who's in charge," Norman says, but the commitment to a more affordable Texas remains the same.

"There's a lot we can get done with the new folks coming in," he says.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5701. Phaze raises $8.75M to give AI agents remote access to powerful workstations

If autonomous artificial intelligence agents are really going to become the future of the enterprise then they’re going to need to have a computer of their own so they can get on with their work without disturbing anyone else.

The founders of the remote desktop firm Parsec Technologies Inc. have come up with a new offering that’s designed to give those agents the computer access they need. Their new startup is called Phaze Inc., and it has just launched its offering after raising $8.75 million in seed funding from Andreessen Horowitz. Today’s round also saw participation from Index, NextView, Makers and Lerer Hippeau.

Phaze has developed a high-performance remote desktop platform that’s designed to accommodate both humans and AI agent workers, giving them access to powerful computers, including high-end workstations. With its platform, those users can control a distant workstation with the same low-latency responsiveness and visual fidelity they’d get if they were accessing hardware locally.

The startup says it’s trying to solve a couple of glaring efficiency problems at many enterprises. One issue is the emergence of computer-use agents that like to hijack worker’s screens while automating mundane business tasks, reducing human productivity.

Another challenge is that many enterprises invest in powerful workstations capable of rendering complex 3D graphics and compiling massive codebases that can cost upwards of $10,000. Those machines are needed, but many information technology departments tend to have a policy of assigning one machine to each employee, which means that expensive hardware is often left sitting idle if that person goes out for lunch, sits in a meeting or takes a few days off.

Phaze’s solution is to transform those workstations into a shared pool of elastic compute, allowing anyone at an organization to access it via its proprietary low-latency streaming technology when they need it. This streaming tech is backed by a specially developed Model Context Protocol server that allows computer use agents to log into and operate expensive workstations the same way a human employee would.

The result: Instead of working exclusively through expensive and brittle application programming interfaces, agents can access a computer directly and navigate its operating system, launch applications and get work done.

Phaze co-founder and Chief Executive Benjy Boxer said the platform also supports human-to-agent collaboration, so they can work together to get more complex tasks done. For instance, an automated IT support bot might work to diagnose problems when new tickets are created, and then pass the session to a human engineer if the solution is more nuanced than what it’s authorized to do by itself.

“The computer sitting on your desk shouldn’t determine what compute you can access,” Boxer said. “People need powerful workstations to do their jobs, and now AI agents need computers they can actually operate. We’re building the access layer that lets either one connect to the machine they need, wherever it happens to be.”

By transforming expensive workstations into shared infrastructure, administrators can assign their computing resources dynamically to whoever needs access as people’s and agent’s workflows fluctuate. The workstations themselves can be sat on a desk, installed in a data center, or locked away in a cupboard. Wherever they’re located, organizations will be able to get maximum efficiency out of them.

Phaze’s job now is to convince enterprises of the benefits of its platform, and Boxer said the money from today’s round will be used to accelerate its go-to-market plans and onboard new customers. The startup will also look to expand its engineering team and develop more features.

Andreessen Horowitz General Partner Martin Casado think Phaze is likely to see a lot of interest in its remote access platform, because workstations are too expensive to be left sitting idle for hours at a time. “Phaze is turning those machines into shared infrastructure for people and AI agents,” he said. “Benjy and the team have been building in this space for more than a decade and they bring that experience to a new era of remote access and machine management.”

#5700. Jobs Jump in October, With Unemployment Dipping Slightly

A day after the stock market hit the skids big-time, there was good news on the employment front. U.S. employers hired at a vigorous pace in October, adding 165,000 jobs, way above the 65,000 forecast, while the unemployment rate lowered slightly to 4.1% from 4.2%.

The report from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics shows that employers are continuing to hire workers even with the Iran War raising energy prices, tariffs a continual worry and the uncertainty of how AI will affect businesses on many levels.

The total nonfarm payroll rise of 165,000 jobs is higher than the average monthly gain of 48,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment increased in professional and business services, in healthcare and in transportation and warehousing.

“Today’s report was impressive,” said Realtor.com® Senior Economist Jake Krimmel. “Coming in, we would have been happy with the forecasted 65,000, more than double last month’s. Instead we got more than double. Revisions added another 84,000 jobs to August and September, lifting the three-month average to 137,000 from about 51,000 a month ago.

“This is still a low hire, low fire market overall, but we could be seeing some green shoots on the hiring side. The numbers could still be revised, of course, and the trend matters more than any one point; but you don’t get a good trend without a good month.”

The report might be a welcome sign for the broader economy one day after stocks plummeted, with AI-centric companies hit hardest. For housing markets, though, the stability comes with a caveat—inflation is likely more of a primary concern for policymakers.

Krimmel noted that for the Fed, the report clears the way for a rate hike, because a soft jobs report was the one thing that could have complicated December.

“If Fed hawks were waiting to exhale, they can do so now,” he said. “One question that keeps coming up is whether the midterms changed anything for the housing market. In the short run, not much—the Iran War and its impact on inflation and mortgage rates remain the major wildcard. Getting back to ‘normal’ in many metros takes more activity, which depends on improved buying power to bring buyers off the sidelines.”

Krimmel noted that mortgage rates have declined for three straight weeks after a massive 74 basis point surge from late August to mid-October, but wages are the other half of buying power.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5699. Mortgage Calculator: Here’s How Much You Need To Buy a $430K Home at a 7.18% Rate

Mortgage rates retreated to a new one-month low this week as bond yields softened in the wake of the historic midterm elections in which Democrats reclaimed control of the House and Senate.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans drifted down to 7.18% for the week ending Nov. 5, down 6 basis points from 7.24% the prior week, according to Freddie Mac. This marks the third consecutive week of easing borrowing costs, providing ongoing relief after rates touched three-year highs last month.

Even with this retreat, borrowing costs remain higher than they were a year ago, when rates averaged 6.22% during the same period in 2025.

So what does this mean for homebuyers? Using the Realtor.com® mortgage calculator, we can look at how the math works out for the median-priced home in the U.S.

All examples assume a 30-year fixed mortgage and include principal and interest only, excluding property taxes, homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance.

For a homebuyer eyeing the median house price of $430,000, a 20% down payment results in a loan amount of $344,000.

At today's 7.18% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment is approximately $2,330. This reflects a $14 monthly reduction from the previous week’s payment of $2,344.

Compared to the 6.22% average from November 2025, which required a $2,111 monthly payment for a home at this price, today’s buyers are paying $219 more every single month.

The monthly costs have also risen markedly for those using FHA loans with a 3.5% down payment.

On a $430,000 home, an FHA borrower would finance roughly $414,950. At today’s 7.18% rate, the monthly principal and interest payment comes to approximately $2,811.

This reflects a $17 decrease from last week's monthly cost of $2,828. Compared to the 6.22% rates of November 2025, where the monthly payment for this loan amount sat at $2,547, today’s FHA borrowers are paying an extra $264 in interest every month.

However, looking back at the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, where the payment for a home at this price reached $2,984, today's monthly payment still offers $173 in relative relief.

The long-term financial picture shows how this continued downward drift improves overall borrowing costs over a 30-year term.

A buyer with a 20% down payment at today’s 7.18% rate will pay a total of $838,935 in principal and interest over the life of the mortgage.

While current financing costs remain above year-ago levels, this total still represents a distinct contrast to the October 2023 peak of 7.79%, when the total cost for that same $344,000 loan would have reached $890,630. By securing a mortgage at today’s rate instead of that peak, a homebuyer effectively avoids $51,695 in interest charges over the 30-year loan life.

FHA borrowers see a similar trajectory of long-term figures. Financing the current median-priced home at today's 7.18% rate results in a lifetime payment of $1,011,966 for principal and interest.

If that same loan had been locked in at the 7.79% peak in late 2023, the total cost would have climbed to $1,074,323. This represents a total long-term savings of $62,357 for FHA buyers.

While the gap above 2025 rates continues to weigh on overall affordability, the steady decline over the past three weeks is helping to restore some predictability and savings for active fall buyers.

#5698. Ocient raises $100 million as agentic AI drives growth in large-scale analytics

Ocient Inc., the maker of a speedy data analytics platform, today said it has raised $100 million in a Series C funding to expand its agentic artificial intelligence analytics business.

That business is fueled by growing demand from national security organizations and telecommunications providers seeking to analyze massive datasets without sampling. The new round brings the Chicago-based company’s total funding to $260 million.

Ocient said it expects revenue to more than triple in its current fiscal year, which ends in January, after doubling revenue the previous year. The company said the new financing will accelerate delivery of its OcientAIQ Solutions, which enable AI agents and human analysts to query petabyte-scale datasets.

Chief Executive John Morris said much of the growth is coming from new customers in national security and telecommunications, particularly organizations using the platform to consolidate cybersecurity information.

“They’ve been accustomed to having to sample data coming off the network,” Morris said. “They don’t have anything that can handle the ingest rates, nor that can store at an affordable price tens of petabytes of data.”

Ocient’s original business focused on high-performance analytics, but the emergence of AI agents has expanded its potential market. Increasingly, software agents rather than human analysts are querying its systems, driving higher utilization and creating demand for more comprehensive datasets.

The OcientAIQ Unified Data Platform combines ingestion, analytics, governance and agent orchestration. Its architecture minimizes data movement and uses forward error correction instead of conventional replication to provide data protection with reduced storage overhead.

“The architecture is designed not to move data around constantly as most architectures do, and to have nothing replicated,” Morris said.

The company competes with Snowflake Inc., Databricks Inc. and open-source analytics implementations, although its technology frequently complements existing platforms rather than replacing them, the CEO said.

Cybersecurity has emerged as a particularly promising market. Ocient provides the underlying data infrastructure that enables security tools and AI agents to analyze network activity across complete historical datasets, potentially identifying threats that conventional sampling would miss.

However, Morris said the company isn’t positioned as a cybersecurity tool. “We don’t do the detection algorithms and the sort of things that the companies in that space do,” Morris said.

Government and defense customers account for a substantial portion of Ocient’s business. The company recently established a dedicated national security subsidiary to serve those markets.

Morris said the new funding should be sufficient to help Ocient reach breakeven, although he declined to provide a timetable. Ocient plans to direct much of the investment toward hiring sales and customer delivery personnel while continuing engineering development.

The company is also seeing increasing demand for on-premises deployments as customers seek greater control over costs and sensitive information. “Most of our opportunities now are on-prem because they’re either repatriating for cost reasons or for data sovereignty and data protection issues,” Morris said.

The company is also looking to expand geographically, particularly in Europe, Asia-Pacific and Latin America, while pursuing additional cybersecurity customers.

The round was co-led by Boka Capital Ltd. and OCA Ventures LLC, with participation from previous investors Greycroft Partners LLC, In-Q-Tel Inc., Blue Bear Capital LLC, Buoyant Ventures Management LLC, PSP Partners LLC’s PSP Growth fund and Pritzker Group Venture Capital LLC.

#5697. EXCLUSIVE: Reba McEntire Reveals the Sentimental Style Behind Her Home

Reba McEntire’s home tells a story—and she has a very personal style that brings it all together.

The country star say in her home, she has rodeo and ranching keepsakes, and reminders of her Oklahoma upbringing.

Speaking exclusively to Realtor.com®, McEntire reveals the sentimental approach behind her decorating choices, the household splurges she considers worth every penny, and why she never wants visitors to feel afraid to get comfortable.

“I'm a country girl at heart, and I love having things around me that tell a story,” she says.

For McEntire, that means surrounding herself with belongings that reflect her experiences and the people who matter most to her.

“So when I bring people into my home, I call it my African cowboy home because I've got my pictures from Africa that I took and then I've got my rodeo ranching things that I've had around me all my life,” she explains.

Those personal touches take priority over decorating purely for appearances.

“I've always believed the home ought to reflect the people living in it, not just what somebody thinks looks pretty,” she says.

McEntire’s reflections come as she continues her partnership with Realtor.com, which launched its “Nearly Home” campaign on May 5, 2025.

The sitcom-inspired ads draw on real homebuyers’ experiences, using humor and practical solutions to make the home-buying journey feel more approachable.

In her own home, however, some of the most important belongings are things she could never replace.

“I'm very sentimental, especially when it comes to family keepsakes, pictures, little things that remind me of mom and daddy, of course, memories of growing up in Oklahoma,” she says.

While furniture can come and go, those connections have lasting value.

“You can always buy new furniture, but you can't replace those memories,” she adds.

Her appreciation for home begins the moment she walks through the front door, when she takes a moment to give thanks before settling in.

“Well, I thank the Lord for getting me home safely, and I put down all my stuff and, just get ready for whatever the rest of the day brings,” she shares.

Although family keepsakes are among her most treasured possessions, McEntire also knows the value of investing in everyday comfort.

When it comes to a home splurge that has proved worth every penny, her answer comes easily. “Oh, without a doubt, a comfortable bed,” she says.

For someone who spends time traveling, returning to her own familiar sleeping setup is a pleasure in itself.

“I spent a lot of time traveling, and there's nothing better than coming home and crawling into your own bed with your own pillow,” she explains.

Another purchase that earns her approval is a good ice machine—a fitting choice given her fondness for iced tea, which she names as something she always keeps in the refrigerator.

Her favorite room is equally straightforward: “Kitchen.”

But McEntire’s ideal day at home does not require an elaborate itinerary or much fuss. “I think I'm pretty low maintenance, but that might surprise somebody,” she says.

“I'm the happiest in comfortable clothes, no makeup on, just relaxing out on the back porch.”

That outdoor retreat includes a particular feature she enjoys. “I've got a real cool porch swing, and I don't need a lot of fuss,” she adds.

A few simple comforts are enough to keep her content.

“Give me good company, something good to eat, and a little peace and quiet, and I'm a happy camper,” she says.

That easygoing attitude also informs the decorating choices she avoids. McEntire has little interest in interiors that make people feel as though they need to tiptoe around.

“Anything that makes a house look like you're afraid to sit on the furniture or walk on the carpet,” she says of the decorating approach she would never try.

In fact, her biggest houseguest pet peeve is someone who does not settle in.

“Someone who doesn't make themselves at home, you know, come on in, get comfortable,” she says.

Asked to describe her home in two words, McEntire offers an answer that captures that philosophy: “warm and welcoming.”

The same sense of comfort and belonging underpins the “Nearly Home” campaign, which pairs McEntire’s humor with relatable homebuying situations and tools designed to help people navigate their search.

The campaign launched ahead of McEntire’s role hosting the 2025 Academy of Country Music Awards, connecting with country music fans as the spring home shopping season got underway. McEntire also debuted her newest single live onstage during the awards.

The ads highlight features such as commute filters, which help buyers check drive times from a potential home, and dynamic maps that let them explore factors including lot size and schools. Through familiar challenges and accessible solutions, the campaign aims to make finding a home feel easier—and more fun.

Now, McEntire is bringing her storytelling to NAR NXT in New Orleans. She will appear in the general session, “The Real Deal: Strategy & Storytelling With Reba McEntire,” on Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026, at the Ernest N. Morial Convention Center.

Attendees can visit the Realtor.com booth, No. 700, on the expo floor on Friday, Nov. 6, for a chance to win a meet-and-greet with McEntire following her Saturday session.

Those stopping by the booth on Saturday and Sunday can also enter for a chance to win officially signed Reba merchandise.

#5696. IBM, AMD and Oak Ridge join forces to launch quantum computing error-correction platform

IBM Corp., Advanced Micro Devices Inc. and the Quantum Science Center at Oak Ridge National Laboratory today announced a new quantum error-correction platform that integrates quantum and high-performance computing.

Gaining high performance and correctness in quantum computing requires protecting quantum information from noise. In many cases, researchers have paired quantum computers with classical computers to achieve superior performance for running industry-relevant problems. The challenge today is scaling up these advances with classical computing.

Today’s physical quantum qubits make errors roughly once every few hundred operations. Without correction, errors compound rapidly, rendering long or complex calculations completely untenable. Game-changing algorithms such as Shor’s algorithm for factoring or for molecular-scale simulations in chemistry require billions of error-free operations.

This launch uses a co-design platform for quantum error correction using IBM’s quantum computers, including the 120-qubit Nighthawk with ORNL’s Umbra High-Performance Computing system powered by AMD’s Instinct MI355X graphics processing units and 5th Gen EPYC central processing units.

“ORNL’s strength in high-performance computing, combined with the expertise of our QSC partners – like IBM and AMD – creates an opportunity to push the boundaries of what is possible,” said Director of the Quantum Science Center Travis Humble. “With Umbra, we will now test new ideas, evaluate approaches at scale, and build the foundation for more reliable quantum computers.”

Jay Gambetta, an IBM Fellow and director of IBM Research, added that the biggest contributor to today’s research is no longer whether error correction will work on quantum hardware, but how to accelerate and optimize it to build systems scientists can use to tackle problems.

IBM said the Nighthawk’s square-lattice connectivity enables industry-leading speed and real-time control to test error-correction techniques. GPU accelerators, such as AMD’s nodes in the Umbra system, can help with this fine-tuning. The co-design platform connected at Oak Ridge will help explore quantum as part of a broader artificial intelligence and scientific computing infrastructure.

“This new co-design platform for quantum error correction allows us to evaluate different approaches and determine the architectures, software and workflows that will scale,” said Gambetta.

Researchers can measure qubits mid-calculation and act on the results in real time, set the exact timing for the signals that protect the qubits from noise, and see exactly what the hardware ran while working with raw measurement signals. This will provide error-correction research with the raw data needed for the next generation of approaches to build sophisticated capabilities for large systems running real code.

Earlier this year, IBM and ORNL unveiled results showing how workloads running on both quantum and classical computers and the Frontier supercomputer can simulate real magnetic materials and calculate molecular configurations of a promising material for fusion fuel.

The simulation of magnetic materials could lead to breakthroughs in superconductors, more efficient batteries and novel drugs. A promising fusion fuel could provide a stepping stone to abundant energy superior to nuclear fission, which powers current nuclear power plants.

#5695. Exclusive: StrongestLayer launches tools to verify payment requests and block hidden AI instructions

Artificial intelligence email security startup StrongestLayer Inc. today launched two products aimed at email that can move money or manipulate an AI assistant.

The first product, Intent Workflows, can hold payment, payroll and executive account requests for verification before anyone acts on them. Alongside it comes AI Instruction Intercept, which stops hidden instructions in a message before an assistant such as Microsoft Corp.’s Microsoft 365 Copilot reads them

Intent Workflows targets attacks that carry no malware or suspicious link. In vendor email compromise, a criminal takes over a real supplier’s mailbox and sends new bank details inside an existing thread.

StrongestLayer went through 32,052 attacks that got past existing defenses at 45 organizations in the second quarter. Only 3.6% were payment or bank-change requests. Under a loss model built on the Factor Analysis of Information Risk framework, that small slice accounted for more than 98% of the estimated financial exposure. Sender authentication checks were little help, since 94% of those messages passed them.

Traditional email security asks whether a message looks bad, according to Alan LeFort, StrongestLayer’s co-founder and chief executive. “The costliest attacks are built to look fine,” he said. His company looks at what a message is trying to make happen, which for a wire transfer means “verifying the action instead of betting on a verdict.”

StrongestLayer’s detection still screens every message. Intent Workflows adds a hold for the smaller set of requests that can’t be reversed, with each customer deciding whether those requests wait for verification or go to the security team or a process owner.

Customers can also let a request through with a policy banner, which appears only on tracked requests and spells out the company’s own rule, such as “Bank change: call the number on file.” Payments in scope are held whatever the verdict, so a hijacked vendor account can’t get one through by sounding legitimate.

The software compares each payment request with the payee’s history, and customers pick the threshold, whether that is every payment or only those over $5,000. If nothing has changed, the payment owner confirms in one click, in Microsoft Teams or by email. Any change, or a new vendor, means a call to a phone number already on file, and the email isn’t released until the outcome is logged.

Payroll changes are verified the same way, and executive password, multifactor authentication and account recovery resets go to the identity or security team first, even when the request comes in through the help desk.

The release also takes on a newer problem. Researchers at Aim Security Ltd. found the EchoLeak flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot last year, and one crafted email was all it took to get the assistant leaking data.

AI Instruction Intercept reads each message first. A reasoning model checks it for hidden instructions against the customer’s own business context, and only after that does the email reach Copilot, Google LLC’s Gemini or a security classifier. Suspect messages are quarantined by default with an explanation of what each instruction was after.

Email is the one route to an AI assistant that “any outsider can use,” said Joshua Bass, StrongestLayer’s co-founder and chief product officer. He argues the inbox is the first place to stop prompt injection, since all an attacker needs is an address.

Both products are available now for Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace and run alongside a company’s existing email security.

#5694. Massive Job Gains of 165,000 in October Bolster Case for More Fed Rate Hikes

Following a disappointing September, U.S. payrolls came roaring back in October as employers went on a hiring spree, adding 165,000 new jobs and pushing the unemployment rate down to 4.1%.

The latest report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, released Friday, shows nonfarm payroll growth more than doubled initial forecasts.

These stronger-than-expected job figures increase the likelihood that the Federal Reserve will remain laser-focused on inflation and raise interest rates in the coming months.

CME FedWatch currently prices a roughly 77% chance of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) raising the federal funds to a 4%-4.25% range in December, followed by a 65% probability in January.

"After last month’s hot inflation print put the next increase in ‘when’ not ‘if’ territory, a soft jobs report was the one thing that could have complicated December," says Realtor.com® senior economist Jake Krimmel. "If Fed hawks were waiting to exhale, they can do so now."

Work sectors that saw the strongest growth in October included professional and business services, which added 70,000 in jobs, well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 over the past 12 months.

Health care came a distant second, with 42,000 payrolls added, followed by transportation and warehousing (+25,000 jobs), and manufacturing (+19,000).

Meanwhile, the September employment data was revised up by 31,000 jobs, from +29,000 to +60,000, while the employment in August was revised up by 53,000, from +133,000 to +186,000.

With these revisions, employment across these two months combined was 84,000 higher than previously reported.

While calling the latest jobs data "impressive," Krimmel points out that the market is still in a low-hire, low-fire mode overall. However, he says that October's payroll surge could be signaling "some green shoots on the hiring side."

"The numbers could still be revised, of course, and the trend matters more than any one point; but you don’t get a good trend without a good month," adds Krimmel.

For homebuyers, Krimmel says that a more dynamic labor market offers some support; however, to meaningfully improve Americans' purchasing power and boost demand requires wage growth to surpass inflation.

Friday's jobs report showed nominal annual wage growth of 3.1% in October, trailing September's 3.7% inflation rate.

"Nominal wage growth is necessary but not sufficient for real wage gains in this environment, so inflation has to come back down, too," says the economist.

The major wildcard remains the ongoing war in Iran, which has driven up inflation and pushed mortgage rates above 7%.

In this week's midterm elections this week, U.S. voters made it known that they were dissatisfied with the state of the economy by handing Democrats control of the House and Senate while flipping multiple traditional Republican strongholds, including Texas, South Carolina, and Kansas.

Even so, Krimmel says that the results of the elections are unlikely to change much for the housing market in the short run.

"Getting back to 'normal' in many metros takes more activity, which depends on improved buying power to bring buyers off the sidelines," he concludes.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5693. New Laws Could Add an Estimated 103,000 Homes a Year, Study Finds

New state laws to encourage homebuilding could bolster the nation's home production by six figures in coming years—but there’s a small catch.

The American Enterprise Institute tracked 10 state bills passed this year and estimates they could potentially lead to 103,000 new homes a year across the country. It's positive progress to solving the nation's housing supply shortage, which is complicated by red tape.

AEI’s data, though, shows that about half of those housing units are accessory dwelling units, or ADUs. But dozens more bills and legislative efforts put forth this year could bring more progress, AEI said at a housing conference in Washinton, DC, this week.

This has been the “year of the starter home,” said Ed Pinto, co-director of AEI’s Housing Center. Thank the bipartisan 21st Century Road to Housing Act, the largest housing reform package in decades. Americans are broadly concerned about affordability, and many young people have grown pessimistic that owning a home will be attainable.

The two largest contributors are California's AB 956 and Washington state's SB 6026.

California's AB 956 loosens requirements around building ADUs. AEI thinks that could result in 48,000 new units a year. Behind that is Washington state's SB 6026, which allows homes in commercially zoned areas. AEI thinks it could mean 37,000 new homes a year.

Other big contributions come from Idaho's SB 1352, which allows homes on smaller lots and could mean 5,000 new homes a year. Kansas' SB 418 brings similar potential in that state. Maine, Virginia, and North Carolina also passed new pro-housing laws.

Tobias Peter, co-director of AEI’s housing center, noted that doesn't necessarily mean every new home will come to fruition. Other kinds of reforms could also unlock hundreds of thousands more homes a year.

At the same time, AEI released a study that found broad support for changes to housing policy. Two rounds of polls of about 5,000 people this year found about 83% support a state law allowing more affordably priced starter homes on smaller lots in new neighborhoods.

AEI found 61% said they’d rather see a torn-down home replaced with two smaller homes, compared to a larger and more expensive home. But people’s opinions trading housing development versus individual property rights can be complicated.

Two of the most popular pushbacks on housing reform fit into two categories. “Supply skeptics” don’t think more homes will improve affordability. Others oppose change to the character or scale of established neighborhoods. Bur rather than housing reform being a "YIMBY versus NIMBY" debate, AEI pictures a spectrum of reform supporters and skeptics.

Some of the largest efforts have focused on the legal red tape around where homes can be built. For instance, several states have put forth laws to allow homes on smaller lots.

But more legislation is needed to correct the slowing construction of starter homes in the nation. Freddie Mac found the U.S. built an average of 418,000 new starter homes a year in the 1970s, 34% of all new housing starts. By 2020 that fell to 65,000 starts, or less than 10%.

“You really need a local champion, a quarterback who organizes at the state level,” Peter said, noting some successful bills where the governor, lieutenant governor, or a group of legislators shepherd a bill. “And it’s also important you have the evidence in your back pocket to counter some of the narratives."

Affordability also requires local governments to respond—because zoning and building code reform, by and large, happens at the local level.

Local government controls some of the most significant levers of affordability, says Yadira Ramos-Herbert, mayor of New Rochelle, NY. And that city's updates to its zoning code have meant incremental progress over time.

New Rochelle developed a form-based code that allows developers to build with fewer requirements around building use. It also streamlined its approval process for new developments, with some taking as few as 90 days to achieve approvals.

The program has helped it approve 4,500 new homes since 2020. New Rochelle, a winner of the University of Utah's 2026 Ivory Prize for Housing Affordability, has seen its median rent decline as national averages surge.

"Our core objective is to ensure New Rochelle remains affordable, accessible, and economically resilient," Ramos-Herbert tells Realtor.com. "Affordability remains the defining challenge of our time, and cities have a responsibility to respond with urgency."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5692. Box taps Nvidia’s AI models to build a rich context layer for autonomous enterprise agents

Few technology firms have embraced the arrival of artificial intelligence agents quite like Box Inc., and today it went even further down the road to automation with an expanded partnership with Nvidia Corp.

At its annual customer conference BoxWorks 2026, Box debuted a new retrieval engine that’s powered by Nvidia’s AI models and designed to give AI agents the much-needed context they require to get more work done. It was announced alongside a new orchestration tool for multistep agentic workflows and new threat detection tools designed to safeguard organizations from rogue agents.

Box’s flurry of announcements are designed to fix a growing bottleneck in enterprise AI workflows. As Box Chief Executive Aaron Levie explained, autonomous agents are only as useful as the context they’re fed allows them to be. If AI agents lack context, they’re going to make mistakes, and that means enterprises simply won’t trust them to do any work, stalling adoption.

Levie said that much of the context that AI agents need does not reside in clean, structured databases, but rather deep inside organizations’ messy troves of unstructured data – things such as contracts, software documentation, policy manuals, internal emails, customer communications records and research archives. Companies know that’s the case, but they’re wary about letting autonomous agents jump right into their data. What’s needed is a way to give those agents secure, permission-aware access to this data, so they’re not looking at things they’re not authorized to see or accidentally leaking secrets all over the internet.

This is where Box’s new partnership with Nvidia intends to make a difference. The company today introduced a new tool called Box Content Retrieval, which is a data retrieval engine that transforms messy enterprise content into a structured knowledge base that agents can access more easily and reason over. It was built using Nvidia’s specialized Nemotron Retriever embedding models, which help to create a neat index of unstructured content like scanned documents, images, audio and video files using multimodal and hybrid search techniques.

Box said Box Content Retrieval is able to improve search accuracy by 20% while reducing token consumption by up to 90%, enabling AI agents to find the context they need to improve their response times to worker’s questions by around four-times. It also makes sure that each AI agent adheres to the native file permissions for each piece of content, so they’re never able to access files their users don’t have permission to see.

“By partnering with Nvidia we are creating a new intelligence layer for enterprise content that gives customers faster, more precise ways to ground AI in the content that powers their business,” Levie said.

The new partnership also sees Box bringing Nvidia’s frontier open-weight models to the table, including the new Nemotron 3 Ultra large language model. These models are directly available within Box AI, and because they’re open-weight, they can be accessed at much more affordable prices than proprietary models from companies like Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC.

Nvidia’s open-weight models have been trained on the domain-specific knowledge for highly specialized workflows, Levie said. For instance, financial analysts can use Nemotron Ultra 3 to query loan applications with strict data-access boundaries, while legal teams can use it to identify contract precedents within corporate agreements by understanding their conceptual meaning rather than searching for keyword matches.

“Open weight is an important part of our vision, complementing closed models while driving innovation and broader adoption across the industry,” Levie added.

Holger Mueller of Constellation Research told SiliconANGLE that Box’s partnership with Nvidia bodes well for the company because the chipmaker is by far and away still the world’s leader in AI platforms, and it will allow it to integrate more closely with the leading public cloud providers too. “Documents are a treasure trove for AI in general and context specifically, and enterprises are very keen to tap into them so they can develop better AI applications,” the analyst said. “This confirms the theory that data has to move to the compute in the AI era.”

Box’s AI push isn’t totally reliant on Nvidia. Indeed, it has its own thing going on with Box Architect, a new tool that will launch in beta later this year, allowing business workers to build, test and deploy new agentic processes using their natural language. According to Box, it can connect to native Box tools such as Extract, Automate, Apps and Forms to create complex workflows, with a selection of open and closed models.

Using Box Architect, law firms will be able to build contract review workflows that are informed by their previously-approved playbooks for past agreements, so that they can compare incoming contracts against it. Should it flag any high-risk clauses, these can immediately be sent to an attorney for review. Alternatively, a bank might use Box Architect to build a streamlined client onboarding workflow that collects applications through Forms, verifies identity documents with Extract and then generates and signs an agreement with Doc Gen and Sign.

Deep Analysis analyst Alan Pelz-Sharpe said these are the kinds of coordinated, autonomous workflows that can make a real difference in terms of the value enterprise AI provides. “While legacy approaches require brittle point-to-point configurations for extraction and execution, an integrated agentic design layer dynamically orchestrates content understanding, process steps and analytical visualization within a single governed ecosystem,” he said.

Box also understands that organizations are going to need more security to protect these more advanced and capable AI agents, which is why it’s simultaneously introducing new threat detection capabilities across its platform. The company said the new security tools make it possible to identify the actions of rogue AI agents in real-time, so that if any of them start exfiltrating data in bulk, deleting massive numbers of files, or taking over user accounts, they’ll immediately be flagged for review.

For instance, administrators will be able to control what files each agent can access through classification-based policies, constrain agent’s actions with MCP guardrails that dictate which third-party tools each one can use, and then detect harmful activities that exceed predefined limits.

#5691. What the Silver Tsunami Means if You’re Planning To Sell

If you’re following the housing market, you may have heard the term “silver tsunami” lately. It’s the idea that millions of homes owned by older Americans could come onto the market as more homeowners reach retirement age and make their next move.

And when you hear a phrase like that, it’s easy to picture a flood of houses hitting the market all at once. But that picture doesn’t match the data.

And if you’re planning to sell, it’s not a reason to put your plans on hold. Let’s look at what the research actually says.

According to Realtor.com, about 13.9 million homes owned by older Americans are expected to change hands by 2036. Sure, that’s a big number. But these homes aren’t all expected to come onto the market at once.

The projections show this happening gradually over the next decade, with roughly 1.3 to 1.5 million homes changing hands each year (see graph below):

Rather than a sudden wave of houses flooding the market, this is a gradual shift as longtime homeowners make decisions about where and how they want to live.

The term silver tsunami makes for a dramatic headline, but the actual data tells a much less dramatic story. And there’s another reason these homes won’t overwhelm the market.

After the 2008 housing crash, builders significantly slowed construction. And for years afterward, they didn’t build enough homes to keep up with demand. That led to a housing shortage we’re still dealing with today.

And just how big a gap are we talking about? Estimates vary, but many experts say the U.S. is still millions of homes short. For example, a recent report from the White House Council of Economic Advisers explains:

“If homebuilding and the growth of the single-family housing stock had continued at their historical pace instead of falling dramatically after 2008, there would be 10 million or more additional single-family homes today.”

As more longtime homeowners sell, those homes will help a gap that’s already there. But they won’t push us over the edge. That’s because, at the same time, more households are expected to form in the decade ahead, and they’ll need homes, too.

So, more homes becoming available over time isn’t automatically a bad thing. It can give buyers more options and help create a more balanced housing market moving forward.

Here’s the takeaway if you’re thinking about selling your house. The silver tsunami isn’t something you need to plan your move around. What’s happening in your local market is far more important than a national projection about the next decade.

That’s because real estate is local. Some markets have more homes for sale than others. Some are seeing houses sell relatively quickly, while others are taking longer.

And those are the conditions that matter when you’re deciding how to price, prepare, and market your house.

For example, an agent who knows your area can help you understand:

How many homes are for sale nearby. This tells you how much choice buyers have and how your house will compare.

What similar houses are actually selling for. That’s one of the most important factors in setting a competitive asking price.

What buyers are looking for right now. Knowing which features and improvements matter most can help your house make a strong first impression.

And that’s something you can act on today, regardless of what happens with the silver tsunami over the next decade.

The right strategy starts with understanding your local market and making decisions based on what’s happening there, not what a dramatic national headline suggests might happen years from now.

The silver tsunami may sound like a major wave of homes coming onto the market, but the research points to a gradual shift over the next decade, not a sudden flood of listings.If you're thinking about selling, don't let that headline make you second-guess your plans. #5690. These Markets Led New-Home Shopper Conversions in Q3

As housing affordability continues to challenge the market and overall shopper activity softens, understanding where prospective buyers are actively engaging becomes increasingly valuable for home building professionals.

Zonda’s latest Homebuyer Outlook shows Houston led major markets for new-home shopper conversions in Q3 2026. Atlanta ranked second, while Riverside rounded out the top three. Atlanta’s performance was particularly notable since the market came in seventh place in Q2 2026.

The results come from Zonda’s proprietary Conversion Index, which gives builders another way to assess buyer interest beyond traffic alone. The index measures the ratio of online shopper clicks to community tour requests on NewHomeSource.com, helping capture the point at which shoppers move beyond researching homes and toward engaging with a community.

While high levels of online shopping can indicate interest in a market, conversions show where consumers are taking a more meaningful action.

That distinction becomes especially useful in a slower demand environment. It also provides another perspective since online shopper activity softened but several markets recorded stronger conversion readings than in the previous quarter. That makes conversion a useful complement to traditional measures of demand.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s Homebuyer Outlook subscription.

#5689. Opendoor Says It ‘Rebuilt’ System With AI, Triples Home Purchases

After over a year of working as CEO, Opendoor’s Kaz Nejatian reported significant growth in revenue and market share during the iBuyer’s Q3 earnings call, and attributed the gains to a shift into AI infrastructure as the company says it has found ways to flip more homes without overpaying.

“This past quarter we rebuilt this entire system at Opendoor. We built an AI system that determines a specific repair plan for every single home before we buy it,” he stated. “Until August, our resale process was similar to literally everyone else in real estate. Pricing every home we owned basically lived in glorified spreadsheets with over 70 columns.”

As real estate incumbents have largely moved on from the iBuying craze that swept over the pandemic boom market, Opendoor has continued to push forward with a more nuanced approach to the model, offering a wider array of services to home sellers and partnerships with agents.

While acknowledging the company still has a long way to go, Nejatian is claiming the turnaround is working, even amid what he characterized as the worst years for housing “in a long time.”

“We’re winning the market without having to make riskier offers,” he said.

A lot of that comes from technology, along with a stronger focus on moving homes faster with less investment. Nejatian pointed out the differences between scaling with employees than with technology. He stated that increasing scale with the traditional method of buying homes involved hiring more employees, and a longer process.

“Rather than having people spending their days looking at pictures and doing mundane tasks, our people now each manage an army of agents,” he added. “In July, we had 5,400 homes. That’s 5,400 sellers sitting in a queue waiting for days for a human to confirm the price on their home. Two weeks ago, that queue was zero, and it will remain zero.”

He also homed in on the iBuyer’s new initiative—Buy with Opendoor—which launched in beta earlier this week. Although the Q3 earnings predates the program’s release, Opendoor CFO Christy Schwartz believes the initiative can open the company up to the broader market.

“Our emerging Buy with Opendoor offering can help buyers whether or not they’re buying a home from Opendoor,” she noted. “We see an opportunity to extend title and escrow to customers who aren’t buying or selling through Opendoor. Similar to listings, the offerings extend our reach beyond our home acquisition business and create opportunities to earn without taking ownership of a home.”

Previously, Nejatian came into the role with an aggressive turnaround mindset, touting an “Opendoor 2.0” initiative to bring the company back to significant profitability. The third quarter earnings may reflect the fruits of his labor, as homes purchased more than quadrupled.

“When a market slows down, companies are left with a cost structure and a system built for a different business. That’s the disease that Opendoor 2.0 is designed to cure,” he added. “That’s why I spend so much of my time on these calls talking about operator efficiency. When we say we’re investing in growth, we are building the capacity to handle the growth that will arrive.”

Overall, Opendoor’s third quarter saw a revenue of $1.02 billion, up 12% from last year’s revenue of $915 million and up 16% from the previous quarter of $883 million.

The number of homes purchased skyrocketed as well, increasing by 316% year-over-year from 1,169 in 2025 to 4,865 in 2026.

At the same time, though, Nejatian acknowledged the company is “behind schedule” on reaching profitability by the end of the year, blaming the slow market.

Opendoor’s stock fell sharply after the report, down about 17% at press time.

Again, Nejatian posited that the increases in efficiency with AI infrastructure have contributed to Q3’s results.

“Not that long ago, around 80% of the assessments we did on homes required an Opendoor employee, which could take many weeks. Today, that 80% is 2%,” he said. “In Q3, we purchased more than four times as many homes as a year ago, and our operation expense was basically the same.”

Operation expenses per acquired home fell to $4,000, down 36% from last year’s expenses of $6,300. The marketing expenses per acquired home dropped at a higher rate, down 57% to $2,800, compared to 2025’s $6,500.

Mortgage originations—or the process in which a borrower goes through to receive a home loan—increased over 400% from quarter-to-quarter, although the Q3 earnings may not reflect the full weight of the Federal Reserve’s rate hike in mid-September. While the latest data does show mortgage rates inching down slowly each week, it’s unclear as to when rates will go below 7%.

“Historically, most of our economics have come from buying and reselling homes complimented by title and escrow,” Schwartz described. “Our emerging mortgage offerings allow us to earn more from each relationship while meeting a critical customer need and making the transaction easier.”

Opendoor’s EBITDA loss also improved slightly on a yearly basis. Q3 2026 had an EBITDA loss of $31 million, while last year had an EBITDA of $33 million. The adjusted EBITDA margin also decreased, now at 3% compared to last year’s margin of 3.6%. While better than last year, Schwartz acknowledged that the latest data is still far off from last quarter’s EBITDA loss of $4 million.

“Most of the sequential decline came from the homes we bought in the spring selling into a much weaker market along with deeper price cuts as we chose to clear rather than hold,” she said.

Looking to the future, Schwartz expects margins to decline again in the fourth quarter, and states that they will continue to sell through the remaining spring acquisitions into Q1 2027.

She also expects revenue to grow by at least 40% on a yearly basis in the next quarter. Although revenue may increase, Schwartz noted that marketing does contain a seasonal aspect, and operating expenses will likely increase due to investments and growth.

“Comparing year-over-year, roughly a third of the increase in our expected loss is the additional marketing, and the remaining two-thirds is primarily higher holding costs as we’ve been rebuilding our inventory,” she concluded.

“Our goal is to be adjusted net income positive on a 12-month-forward basis at the end of this year,” Nejatian continued. “We’re a bit behind on this today, but we’re going to go through some walls and catch up.”
